330325,ca.proc.d.1911-02-16.1.1.1,1911-02-16,,,,stagedirection,,,,"Mr. McLEiVN (Queens) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 118) to amend the
Canada Shipping Act. He said:
column2: The object of this Bill is to amend section 477 of the Shipping Act so that coal barges under tow may come into the ports of Canada without being obliged to pay pilotage fees. Up to a recent decision of the Privy Council, coal barges have been coming into our ports in the maritime provinces without paying pilotage dues. Under this decision it is held that the words in the Act ' ships propelled wholly or in part by steam ' do apply to coal barges under tow. For example, the Cumberland Coal and Railway Company send from Parrsboro' to St. John coal in barges towed by a steam tug, two or three barges in tow; and they have been coming in under the decision of the court as to the meaning of those words I have just quoted, holding that they do apply to coal barges under tow. This decision of the Privy Council holds that they are obliged to pay pilotage. The object is to allow coal barges of that description towed by steam to be exempt from paying pilotage dues.

column1: Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.",,,,

column2: France is a favoured nation country to a limited extent, that is to say, as respects the lists of articles specified in schedules B and C to the French Treaty. Twelve countries:

column1: Austria-Hungary, Bolivia, Colombia, Denmark, Japan, Norway, Russia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland and Venezuela-are accorded most favoured nation treatment generally. These are consequently enjoying the benefits of the French Treaty. As respects the dutiable schedules in the agreement with the United States, the concessions to be granted to the United States are largely the same as already have been granted to France and the favoured nation countries. As respects a large part of the list, therefore, no additional advantage will be enjoyed by such countries. There are however, a few articles in the French schedules which in the agreement with the United States are made free or dutiable at lower rates. In these cases the advantages granted to the United States will extend also to France and the favoured nation countries. In the case of a few articles which are not to be found in the French Treaty the favoured nation countries will be entitled to receive the concessions on the same terms as the United States, but France will not be so entitled. Although not arising from any agreement, in no case has any advantage been granted to any foreign country that did not at the same time extend to all parts of the British Empire. In the few cases in which the rates to be established are lower than those already enjoyed by British countries the reductions will apply to such countries. _

330353,ca.proc.d.1911-02-16.2.8.1,1911-02-16,7b93f979-f291-49f1-9a5c-54d08800f177,ca.m.2348,Mr. SPROULE.,,QUESTIONS.,PELAGIC SEALING.,,Before the orders of the day are called, I wish to call tire attention of - the government to an .item which I see in to-day's ' Citizen ', which reads as follows :

Washington, Feb. 15-Action was taken to-day by the senate committee on foreign relations which if sustained by the senate will not only put an end to pelagic sealing in the Behring sea, but will also stop the killing of seals on shore for a period of years. The committee to-day ordered a favourable report on tbe draft of a treaty between America and Great Britain providing for the protection of seals in this manner. It is based upon tbe declaration of experts that tbe seal herd, now nearly exterminated, will be completely restored to its original strength in the course of a few years if left completely undisturbed. Russia and Japan must also make similar treaties to make this effective.

I would like to inquire of the right hon. the Prime Minister ('Sir Wilfrid Laurier) if such a treaty is being negotiated, and if he can communicate to the House any information regarding it, or upon what lines it proceeds, or tell us if we are bartering away -any rights which we possess in the seal fisheries at the present time.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Thomas Simpson Sproule,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=7b93f979-f291-49f1-9a5c-54d08800f177&Language=E&Section=ALL

term of years of pelagic sealing upon terms which have 'been mutually agreed upon and which, I have no doubt, will be found satisfactory. I am not in a position to-day to put the treaty before the House, but I hope to do so within a short time, and *certainly as- soon as we have received it.

330359,ca.proc.d.1911-02-16.2.9,1911-02-16,,,,subtopic,QUESTIONS.,THE FLAG ON PUBLIC BUILDINGS.,,,,,,
330360,ca.proc.d.1911-02-16.2.9.1,1911-02-16,c1b69015-0348-4ed6-8d8a-3de18e5d1742,ca.m.2824,Mr. HUGHES.,,QUESTIONS.,THE FLAG ON PUBLIC BUILDINGS.,,I desire to bring the attention of the government to the fact that it has never been customary to fly the flag on the public institutions of Canada on St. David's Day. St. David's Day is the 1st March. The white cross of St. David forms a part of our Union Jack and I am satisfied that the people of Welsh descent in Canada will be only too glad to find the government ordering up the flag on public buildings on that day. The eldest son of our Sovereign takes his title as Prince of Wales from that part of the United Kingdom and Welshmen have always been found to the front doing their duty in defence of the empire. I trust the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) will be good enough to order the flag to be flown on public buildings on the 1st March.

,Liberal-Conservative,,Samuel Hughes,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=c1b69015-0348-4ed6-8d8a-3de18e5d1742&Language=E&Section=ALL
330361,ca.proc.d.1911-02-16.2.9.2,1911-02-16,d450f513-61eb-48c4-b15a-6c4a45717765,ca.m.8049,Mr. PUGSLEY.,Minister of Public Works,QUESTIONS.,THE FLAG ON PUBLIC BUILDINGS.,,The suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes) will receive due consideration. While the question of flying the flag on public buildings is before the House I might refer to a question put by an hon. gentleman a short time ago. He asked me for information with regard to flying the flag throughout Canada. There are certain days, with which hon. gentlemen are no doubt familiar, upon which the flag is always flown upon all the public buildings, and then it may .also be flown upon other days to be named by the Minister of Public Works. Latterly the question has come up with reference to flying the flag upon public buildings upon every day in the year. It has been thought that would be a somewhat expensive matter, and, therefore, it would be worthy of some consideration before deciding to do it. In an informal way I have conferred with my colleagues upon this subject, and they Sir WILFRID LAURIER.

approve of the suggestion that in the border cities and towns, including the seaports of Canada, it would ibe desirable to have the flag flown every day in the year. The reason for that is that the United States flag is flown upon the American consulate every day in the year. It was a matter of remark in the city of St. [DOT]John that a stranger coming by steamer to the city, upon whatever day he came, saw the Stars and Stripes flying to the 'breeze and unless it happened to be a special occasion he would not see the Union Jack. Therefore, in the seaports to which strangers are constantly coming, and in the border towns I have directed that the flag shall be flown upon our public buildings every day in the year. With regard to having it flown upon all public buildings in Canada upon every day in the year, that is a matter that is still under consideration.

PUGSLEY (Minister of Public Works).,Minister of Public Works,QUESTIONS.,RENTAL OF OTTAWA BUILDINGS- LIGHTING CONTRACT.,,Mr. Speaker, I desire to rise to a question of privilege. In the Evening ' Journal,' published in the city of Ottawa last evening, I find a statement prepared lay Mr. Ellis, the treasurer of the city of

Ottawa, and who is the head of the municipal lighting department of the city. Referring to certain statements which I made in the House with reference to the lighting of certain buildings owned .by the Imperial Realty Company, Mr. Ellis is reported as making the following remarks :

On my return from Toronto a few days ago I found that the Hon. Dr. Pugsley had in the House of Commons charged me with having issued false vouchers in connection with the electric light consumed by his department in the buildings rented from Mr. Woods.
I emphatically say that no vouchers or accounts, false or otherwise connected with this matter were ever issued by me, or on my instructions, or with my knowledge.

When the department became a tenant of Mr. Woods, he had a flat rate from the Consumers' Company. The department was offered but refused a flat rate, and determined to pay according to the meter rate. It then requested Mr. Woods to instruct the Consumers' Company to place meters in the building in order to measure the current. The company complied with this request, for the sole purpose of enabling the Public Works Department to be furnished officially with correct statements of the amount which they had agreed to pay. Mr. Woods had nothing to do with the meter readings. He had a flat rate with the Consumers' Company and he continued it.

The position therefore was that Mr. Woods, as landlord of the buildings, had a flat rate with the Consumers' Company, and the department, as tenant, desiring to pay according to the amount of electricity which it should actually consume, obtained installation of meters and required for its own information quarterly statements taken from the meters. These statements were furnished by the Consumers' Company until the city took oyer its plant, and since then have been furnished by the city. There is no other way in which the department could have been informed as to what it ought to pay. Neither the Consumers' Company nor the city need have taken the trouble which they did to give the department the information which it desired to have. Both did it merely as a business courtesy, and the return which the city gets is a recklessly untruthful villifica-tion.

In March, 1906, the city offered to give the Department of Public Works direct, Mr. Woods' flat rate contract, but this offer was not accepted, the department thus refusing a flat rate for the second time. The government therefore could from that time have had a contract direct with the city at the same rate which Mr. Woods paid the city, but instead continued paying him the full meter rates. If Mr. Woods has made a profit in the meter out of the government the Public Works Department is alone to blame.

Mr. Pugsley has no justification whatever for the statements he made regarding myself or for bringing my name into the matter at all. In fact, _ he had information at his disposal at the time he made the statements which conclusively showed this.

The remarks which I made and to which Mr. Ellis refers will be found on page 3240 and following of ' Hansard.' I have looked over the statement I made and I have nothing to add to and nothing to retract from that statement, except in one respect. I find that upon page 3240 I stated that when I became minister there was rendered to my department by the Imperial Realty Company bills upon a meter basis.

I stated, further, that these bills were rendered by the company, that they were accompanied by bills on their regular account forms rendered by the electric light department of the city of Ottawa, presided over by the city treasurer, Mr. Ellis, showing the indebtedness of the Imperial Realty Company, or James W. Woods, as the case might be, to the city for the amount of current consumed based upon the meter rate, and that these bills were marked ' settled ' by the electrical department of the city, that they were receipted as vouchers, and that they accompanied the bills which the Imperial Realty Company rendered to my department. You will observe, Mr. Speaker, that I stated that these bills had been rendered by the electrical department of the city of Ottawa. I did not mention Mr. Ellis's name then, although I knew that Mr. Ellis was the gentleman who presided over that department, and who I would suppose would be responsible for vouchers or bills that would be issued bv that department. A little later in the discussion, as will be seen by page 3241 of ' Hansard,' the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe! referred-to Mr. Ellis-and this was the first mention that was made of Mr. Ellis's name in that connection, as follows:

330386,ca.proc.d.1911-02-16.2.11.18,1911-02-16,d450f513-61eb-48c4-b15a-6c4a45717765,ca.m.8049,Mr. PUGSLEY.,Minister of Public Works,QUESTIONS.,RENTAL OF OTTAWA BUILDINGS- LIGHTING CONTRACT.,,Yes, it is true as I stated, and as is found in ' Hansard,' that away back in 1904, before I became minister.

when the question was put to Mr. Ewart, chief architect, as to whether he would prefer to pay by the meter or flat rate, he preferred the meter rate, because he said the department would prefer to pay for the electric light actually consumed. But so far as the records show, at all events during the years that I have been in charge of the department, it does not appear that the government was paying one cent more for electric light than the city was charging Mr. Woods or the Imperial Realty Company, that, in other words, the accounts show that the department was paying to the Imperial Realty Company the identical amounts which the city was charging for the electricity consumed. You will observe that these accounts show that they were settled by the Imperial Realty Company, and so the accounts go along all in the same way. A little later on I find in the very last account rendered a statement exactly in the same form upon the bill-heads of the municipal department of the city. Here is a statement of what it was alleged by the city Mr. Woods was indebted to them for lighting, and on it there is this statement. ' Settled by cheque, Municipal Electric Department,' signed by Mr. Pennock. That is a little stronger than these others, because there is here an allegation that a cheque had been given by Mr. Woods to the city of Ottawa for the identical amount which Mr. Woods was charging to the Department of Public Works.

Mr. Rllis refers to the -three buildings The evidence before the Committee on Public Accounts discloses that in respect to the Queen street building the city of Ottawa was paid by a meter rate and not by a flat rate, and if you take the accounts from beginning to end, you will find that the city dealt with the lighting of the Queen street building in exactly the same way as it did with the lighting of the buildings on Slater street, so far as the issuing of these accounts and vouchers was concerned.
Mr. Ellis says:
In March, 1906, the city offered to give the Department of Public Works direct, Mr Woods' flat rate contract, but this offer was not accepted, the department refusing a flat rate for the second time.

I have examined the records of the department and I cannot find a trace of any such offer having bee'n made. No offer was made, so far as I have been able to discover, but I do admit that in 1904, and I so stated when I addressed the House previously upon this question, the department, through Mr. Ewart, had the opportunity of paying for lighting by meter or flat rate, and it preferred to. pay by a meter rate, but there is nothing to show

that the officials of the department knew that Mr. Woods was receiving anything from the Public Works Department beyond what he was paying to the city of Ottawa, and I wish to emphasize the statement which I have already made that I cannot conceive how it is possible for Mr. Ellis to be mistaken in regard to these accounts. It may be that he did not see the accounts which were rendered by an official of his department, who is acting under his supervision, it may be that they were issued in entire ignorance upon his part, but that they were issued and were presented as vouchers from time to time there can be no doubt, as appears from the vouchers as they appear in the report of the Committee on Public Accounts, and as they appear also in the records of the department.

I ought to call the attention of you and of the House to what took place upon the 23rd of May, because I think I will show that the official of the municipal department recognized that what he had done had misled the Department of Public Works. Upon the 23rd of May, 1910, I wrote this letter, addressed to the mayor of the city of Ottawa:

Dear Mr. Mayor,-During the recent session of parliament it was stated by a member of the Public Accounts Committee, who professed to know, that the government was paying a considerably larger amount for the lighting of buildings owned by the Imperial Realty Company, Limited, in this city, than was actually charged by the city.

Yu looking over the accounts, I find that the Municipal Electric Department of the city furnished from time to time bills charging the company meter rates, and which bills were for the same amounts, as paid by the department. These accounts were submitted as vouchers, and the proper officials of my department, as well as the Auditor General, acted upon these vouchers, presuming that they were correct, and paid the hills.

As an illustration, I find that an account was rendered by the Imperial Realty Company on the 22nd September, 1909, a copy of which is attached. Accompanying the account are vouchers, copies of which are also hereto annexed. These accounts are marked ""Settled by the Imperial Realty Company,"" and are signed by the Municipal Electric Department.

I shall esteem it a favour if you will kindly advise me as to whether or not my information in regard to there being a difference between the amounts paid to the city, and the amounts of the vouchers, signed on behalf of the city, is correct, and, if so, I shall be glad to have such explanation as the officials of the city have to offer upon the subject.
I am, dear Mr. Mayor,
Yours very truly,
(Sgd.) WILLIAM PUGSLEY. Charles Hopewell, Esq.,
Mayor, Ottawa.

And this is the letter of Mr. Pennock, the accountant of the Municipal Electric Department, an official under Mr. Ellis, to His Worship the Mayor:
Ottawa, June 3rd, 1910.
His Worship,
Mayor Hopewell,
City.
Dear Sir,-I have your letter of May 27th, regarding a letter received by you from the Minister of Public Works in reference to account for electric current furnished to the Woods Building.

You say that the Minister of Public AVorks asks: 'Whether his information in regard to there being a difference between the amounts paid to the city and the amounts of the vouchers signed on behalf of the city is correct, and also if such be the fact what explanation can be given.'
In reply I beg to say,-

Mr. Woods pays the city for the Queen street Building the regular meter rates and for the Woods and Canadian Buildings, the fiat rate. I am informed that his agreement with the government provides that they shall pay him on a regular meter rate for all the buildings. The meter rates are invariably higher than the flat rates. In order to enable him to render his account to the government on the meter basis, meters were installed in these buildings and meter readings have been regularly made, first by the Consumers Company and afterwards by the city.
The practice of installing meters for this purpose was commenced in 1904 before I was employed by the company.

The accounts referred to in the minister's letter were made up from such meter readings and for the purpose only of enabling Mr. Woods to render to the government his accounts upon the regular meter rate.

330393,ca.proc.d.1911-02-16.3.2,1911-02-16,,,,subtopic,WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH UNITED STATES.,,,[""The hon. gentleman must remember that under these circumstances, we would have a preference in the British market, for our products, and that would more than compensate for the small amount of New Zealand butter that might come in. Let the hon. Minister of Railways who is interested in Transportation remember that 77,000,000 tons of freight passed down the River St. Clare last year, and let him remember what the result of this policy will be, our shipping industry will be crippled on the Atlantic ports, on the ports of the Great Lakes and on the Pacific coast. To-day Canada stands at the parting of the ways. For years we have spent our energies towards developing our markets and our tariff has been framed with that object in view, but just as everything is going along smoothly, there comes the cry: we must trade with the United States, and not with Great Britain. It is proposed to dam the trade and commerce of Canada so that it will flow through American ports and channels, break up our commerce with the old land and divert our great trade which

flows east and west to north and south. There are few citizens of Canada, who are not affected adversely by this arrangement entered into by this government to sell our heritage and endanger our national existence. The Finance Minister apd the Minister of Customs who made the agreement, after 14 long years of office without any apparent effort or change in the fiscal policy of the country, have at last found the opportunity to open the door to continental free trade. A tottering government in the United States has entered into an arrangement with a government tottering to its fall in Canada. I believe, Sir, that this is the first step towards the dismemberment of the British Empire. We possess a country so vast and so rich in grain producing and mineral wealth and so advantageously situated that of all the lands on the globe we offer the most favourable outlook of any nation. This land belongs not only to us, but to our children's children, and it is our duty to preserve it intact for their heritage.
We are building a nation and building it our own way and according to our ideals to-day but what of to-morrow?
Our neighbours to the south say: Come in with us, we will help you but you must build as we desire. We answer: Canada is not for sale-our laws are firm, yours are lax. Our marriage vows are sacred, yours are lax. We can control our trusts if our government will only go about it in the proper way while yours are running rampant. We were kicked out of the American market in 1866. Who will say that we cannot be kicked out in 1912? In 1867 we started a system of interprovincial trade, the development of our natural resource^, the creation of home industries, and the disposal of our surplus products in the permanent market of Great Britain.
The government of that day opposed unrestricted reciprocity. They advocated national development, and opposed conti-nentalism. They were right and time has proved it. The United States ignored us then, they are courting us to-day. In 1831 this country registered the course it would follow. This government registered its protest against reciprocity in 1897 when they came back from Washington. The power rests to-day with the United States to cancel this agreement, unrestricted reciprocity means free trade, free trade means direct taxation. Using the words of Sir John Macdonald in 1891: 'Shall we endanger our possession of the great heritage bequeathed to us by our forefathers, and submit ourselves to direct taxation, for the privilege of having our tariff fixed at Washington with a prospect of ultimately becoming a part of the American Union?
Canada is sure of her future, if she remain free, Canada has to-day a trade for her goods outside the United States, Can-119}
ada has to-day a market for her goods outside the United States, Canada is independent of the United States, Canada would not be independent of United States if this treaty went into effect. Our infant industries have had a struggle and have survived without the United States tariff'. In 1910 we sold the United Stares $100,000,000, they sold us $223,000,000. The Canadian tariff is 26 per cent; the United States tariff 42 per cent. This is a sample of Yankee fair trade. I am opposed to this arrangement because it is not consistent with the policy of conserving our natural resources. Are Winnipeg, Toronto, Vancouver, Montreal and other leading cities and towns throbbing with life and activity to be content, with the left over trade of the United States.
Quebec, Halifax and St. John cities which the Grand Trunk Pacific were to help will be sidetracked and the trade go and come through the United States. Why disrupt our general business conditions, disturb the activities of our cities, lessen the earning power of our trunk lines of railroads if we are to be a united people with common political ideals and aspirations? Let us throw out this measure.
As a people we are only emerging from childhood; let us leave well enough alone. As Canadians for Canada let us guard well the political destiny of our future.
There is no use offering amendments to the deal, any change would nullify the whole agreement. Canada by adopting this policy will bid a long farewell to her greatness, and as the handmaid of the American trusts, contribute the 51st Star to the flag which will control the continent. It is the work of little Canadians. I belong to a nation to-day that is full of hope and prospect. In a few weeks if this measure passes the future of this country will be fixed. The wealth of our forest are the heritage of our workingmen and capitalists alike.
The labour interests of our cities and towns are vitally affected. You send the raw material to United States to be finished instead of at home. Let us keep the raw products at home and employ our own men in preparing them for the market. Taft cannot wait. The United States government say ' Canada dig your ore, send it to us and we will refine and perfect it. Canada give up your raw materials, and we will finish them and export the finished product.'
If you pass this Bill you will lead us back to pre-confederation days when the eastern provinces traded with the eastern States, Ontario with New York and the western States and British Columbia traded with the States on the western coast. You have sold the salt men, meat men, the fruit men, the manufacturers, the financier, the railroad, the lake freighter, labour man and farmer. These men""]",,,,

330394,ca.proc.d.1911-02-16.3.2.1,1911-02-16,5bfd2fe5-bfe6-42c4-9503-71c3b6f865df,ca.m.5370,Mr. HAUGHTON LENNOX (South Simcoe).,,WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH UNITED STATES.,,,"I am glad to see that the very general attendance of members on this side indicates the deep interest the Conservative party are taking in this question. It is no wonder that this should be the case because never during the past 15 or 20 years, or perhaps a-longer period,-has-anything been presented to this House which will probably have such far reaching consequences as the resolution now before us. I paid very careful attention to the very able address made yesterday by my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), and if I have to take exception to that address, it will not at all be as to the fluent and eloquent way in which he presented his argument, but rather to the attitude assumed and his failure to carry out the promise he made in opening his speech. After making a very elaborate and carefully prepared statement of figures and drawing from them many somewhat strained and difficult conclusions, he closed his address by saying that in the bargain made between Canada and Washington, every interest affected had been guarded both as regards this country and Great Britain. I submit that my hon. friend will hardly be prepared to stand by that proposition if he gives the matter a moment's reflection. Around about the city of Guelph, comprising some 16,000 inhabitants, there are market gardeners and others raising fruit and vegetables-a growing industry- so that he need not go beyond his own riding to ascertain that interests of a very important character have been struck, and struck very hard by the proposed arrangement. In the exuberance of words in which he indulged yesterday, he forgot that within the last week we had within this very chamber some 1,500 representatives of the two important industries of fruit growing and market gardening who protested that their interests were about to be injuriously affected, and he forgot also that the right hon. the Prime Minister had to admit that he was absolutely helpless to assist that large delegation which had so ably pressed on him its views. *

I might multiply instances and point out that, whilst my hon. friend may think this is a matter of comparative insignificance, yet these men represent families probably aggregating 8,000 or 10,000 people; that they employ perhaps tens of thousands of labourers in their industry-which is a growing industry, and in the early stages of its development,-and that the people in the towns and cities which are surrounded by these industries, are receiving large emoluments from dealing with these people. So I submit to you, Mr. Chairman, that this is not a trifling matter to be brushed aside by my hon. friend as beneath his consideration. And it does not end there. Does my hon. friend forget that the whole future of British Columbia is practically sacrificed by the proposals which the government have presented to this House; that, so far from guarding the various interests of this country, the government, or the government's representatives, negotiating behind closed doors, utterly ignored the rights and interest of a Yvhffie^province of this- Dominion-? -

Now, the hon. gentleman saw fit to attack the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax), in a very animated, if not. to say vicious way. He greatly deplored that the leader of the opposition had spoken in reference to the appointment of a tariff commission, and he pointed out that this would be a complete departure from precedent and from the system upon which British countries are usually governed. Not to do the hon. gentleman any injustice, I will read what he said:

No doubt such a plan would meet the desires of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association; but if my hon. friend would adopt such a system, he would be reversing: one of the cardinal principles of British politics, which is that the right to tax must remain with the peoples' representatives. The right was established many long years ago, and I have no doubt will survive to the end; but if the leader of the opposition desires to depart from that principle and appoint a permanent tariff commission to regulate our tariff, the sooner the people should know it the better.
Was that-especially as coming from a gentleman of the ability of my hon. friend -a fair way to present the remarks of the

leader of the opposition ? Did the leader of the opposition propose to rob representatives in parliament of any of their rights; did he ever propose to shackle parliament in the exercise of its powers ? No, Sir. It conies with rather poor grace from a supporter of this order in council government, which has been so actively at work, in this direction, in the last few years to talk of limiting the rights of parliament. But so that we may know exactly how that matter stands, I will read a few lines of what the leader of the opposition really said. And I might call the attention of the committee to the fact that, while my hon. friend was brave enough to start out with the idea of reading the language of the opposition leader, he changed his mind and could not afterwards be got to do it. What the leader of the opposition said was this:
Upon what should our policy he based ? Should it be based upon an attempt to create millionaires in this country or to impose unfair conditions upon any portion of the community?

Not by any means. Does my hon. friend object to that proposition? I believe that we in Canada, in the future still more than in tiie past, should attempt to shape our tariff upon scientific consideration of known facts. I believe it would be well that we should have exact information as to these matters laid before parliament. I believe it would be well if we established a permanent tariff commission in Canada so that our tariff should not he made by rule of thumb. An agitation arises in some part of the country against a duty of 25 per cent, and it is said it should be reduced to 15 per cent, and the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Customs get together and the industries affected declare in stringent tones that a reduction of 15 per cent would absolutely wipe out their industry, and throw thousands of men out of employment, and then the Minister of Customs and the Minister of Finance say: We will compromise, and we will make it 20 per cent. I do not think that is the manner in which onr tariff should he framed; I think it should aim at equalization of cost of production so far 'as that can reasonably be accomplished. We ought to give the people of this country a fair opportunity to create industries and to give employment, but we ought not to give it under conditions as would impose burdens upon a portion of our people.

Does my hon. friend object to that proposition which he would not read ? He seems to think that we should not consider the Manufacturers' Association. He had his little fling at this side of the House, in connection with that matter. Therefore, I can assume, surely, that neither he nor any hon. gentleman on that side of the House has been coquetting with the Manufacturers' Association upon this subject. Let us see what the records show. There was a meeting of the Manufacturers' Association in Montreal in October, 1908.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Haughton Lennox,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=5bfd2fe5-bfe6-42c4-9503-71c3b6f865df&Language=E&Section=ALL
330395,ca.proc.d.1911-02-16.3.2.2,1911-02-16,5bfd2fe5-bfe6-42c4-9503-71c3b6f865df,ca.m.5370,Mr. LENNOX.,,WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH UNITED STATES.,,,At that meeting, several distinguished members of this House were present. A gentleman addressing the banquetters said:

It is in this spirit that I am authorized to state to you, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, that while we recognize that the responsibility rests upon the government of the day of settling the tariff, this association will heartily welcome the establishment of a permanent tariff commission, to which the multifarious details that enter into the tariff question must he referred for investigation and report. Such a suggestion does not flow from any desire to infringe upon the rights of parliament or to restrict its responsibilities, hut rather to aid it by bringing to hear upon the difficult and complicated tariff problems which are constantly calling for consideration, the fullest possible light from every possible quarter.

What the leader of the opposition proposed was, that we should not be dealing with this question in the dark, that we should have a permanent tariff commission to investigate matters pertaining to the tariff; that they should collect data and that the information which they collected should be reported to parliament so that parliament could intelligently act upon and deal with the question. Well, Sir, I have the opportunity of showing that a reasonably prominent gentleman in the ranks of the government entirely concurred in that view.

There is just another idea as to which I want to have a word of expression. You have stated, Mr. Chairman, in your address, that you desired to have a permanent tariff commission. I do not exactly realize yet what is meant by a ' Permanent Tariff Commisison/ but I am free to say that if it be meant that you would have a permanent commission such as I think they have in the United States to follow the workings of the tariff from day to day, to follow the incidence, to follow the effects upon the producer and the consumer, and its daily effects upon the community, I do not see any reason why such a commission should not be appointed.

That was the statement of the right hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier. But he did not stop there; as he so often says, ' that is not all,' because he also pointed out to them that he had decided to appoint a commission, which would not be composed of politicians or party heelers, but of business men and of experts, to make inquiry in foreign countries. And that was not all, either. He told these gentlemen whom my hon. friend is so much afraid of, that if that did not satisfy them, he was willing to appoint another commission, and he was willing to have them represented upon that commission. So the government, to say the least of it, has gone one better upon that question of a tariff commission.
Now. my hon. friend also thought that the leader of the opposition was very weak

in using the expression ' let well enough alone/ Well, if he had read what the leader of the opposition said as the foundation for that advice, he would have realized that it is pretty sound advice. The leader [DOT]of the opposition had pointed out the policy upon which this country has been built up, with transportation lines running from east to west. He had shown that we had for a great number of years, for forty years, pursued the steady policy of self-reliance, that every industry in this country was practically booming at the present time, and he intimated that in this condition of things, for a shadowy chance of gain it was not wise to make this radical departure. without consulting the people, and it would be wise, perhaps, to leave well enough alone. I want to say. Sir, that 1 believe there is a large majority of people in this country v'ho would echo that sentiment to the full. Why, listen to some facts in addition to those referred to by my honoured leader as showing the prosperity of the country at the present time. Take the building permits, last year they amounted to $94,000,000, and in 1909 to $65,000,000; so there was a net gain in the building industry, indicating the prosperity of the cities, of $29,000,000, or 45 per cent. Back to the farm, said my hon. friend; the rural population is also in a thrifty condition. We must lemember that Ontario is being drained to some extent by the flow of her sturdy sons to the west, yet notwithstanding that- drain, Ontario, according to the last report, has gained

column2: in population iiT Two~ ""years, while the annual products of the farm now amount to $250,000,000. Live stock in Canada, in 1910, was valued at $599,768,000; in 1909 it was valued at $555,879,000. So there has been a net gain in the value of live stock alone of nearly $35,000,0000. Let me give you a summary of other evidence of progress. Since 1868 we have doubled in population; we have enormous American industries planted in Canada, representing $250,000,000; we have more than that number of millions of capital waiting to come to Canada, and halted by reason of the attitude of the government at the present time. The area of Canada under cultivation is ten times what it was in 1868; the hanking capital is ten times what it -was ; deposits in the banks are ""nearly thirty times what they were; our railway mileage is about twelve times what it was, and the freightage is about twelve times what it was in 1868. We have an unexcelled system of railway transportation in Canada; we have a greater railway mileage and greater facilities for carrying our products to the markets of the world, rated per population, than any other country in the world. Therefore, having made this progress in face of the steady opposition of the Americans for forty years, is it not wise, even without regard to what this may lead us to, in a political sense, is it not somewhat wise that we should adopt the motto of leaving well enough alone?

column1: My hon. friend from Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) promised us something that he was not able to carry out; he promised us that his address would be nonpolitical, but he could not keep that promise.
column2: I do not think there is

column1: an hon. gentleman on that side of the House who could redeem a promise of that kind. Within four or five sentences, he had plunged deeply into politics. He did not lash and slash the leader of the opposition to any great extent, but there is one man whose influence upon him cannot be withstood, and that is the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster). So within a few sentences the hon. gentleman got into his old habit, he forgot all his good resolutions, and he plunged deeply into politics, where he wallowed until the end of his address. My hon. friend had a leader whom he could not disregard in that respect; he was only following in the lead of the Minister of Customs, who, after he had uttered four sentences, following the speech of the leader of the opposition, in which not one political sentence is to foe found, in his fifth sentence, plunged into a comparison of the old way and the new- the prosperity of the country was all due to the Reform party-it was all brought about by this magnificent government now in power. I ask you, Mr. Chairman, and von are a fair man, what has that got to do with the matter? How does it affect this great issue, whether our prosperity was brought about by the Liberal party or by the Liberal-Conservative party? It is business we are after, and it is safety we are considering in this matter, and in the consideration of these questions, it is a poor policy to descend tp the discussion of which party has brought about prosperity.

Then my hon. friend referred to geographical conditions-a boundary line of 4,000 miles contiguous to the United States, it was a pity that these geographical conditions should be ignored. In that he is only following the lead of American newspapers The New York ' American ' is very eloquent upon the geographical conditions of the two countries. Do not fight against nature, they say ; it is not right, it is not Christian, it is not kind, it is not wise, and yet for thirty years these same Americans fought against ' geographical conditions ' and the geographical conditions have not changed one iota in these forty years. Then if that is so, we want some better explanation of not fighting against geographical conditions than we have got so far. My hon. friend spoke of the wheat industry. I must say he was

rather fair in that. He said that he did not expect any great quantity of wheat to be exported to the United States, that he did not expect any immediate increase in price, but that he expected a gradual rise. He is contradicted in that by the President Mr. Taft who says that he expects a gradual fall. Mr. Taft has studied this question. The object he lias in view is to lower the cost of living in the United States. If the cost of living is to be decreased by bringing in Canadian wheat, of course, it goes without saying that you must reduce the price of wheat in the United States. Mr. Taft says :
Reciprocity with Canada must necessarily be chiefly confined in its effect on the cost of living to food and forest products.
_He says again :

I do not wish to hold out the prospect that the unrestricted interchange of food products will greatly and at once reduce their cqst to the people of this country. Moreover, the present small amount of Canadian surplus for export as compared with that of our own, production and consumption would make the reduction gradual. Excluding the element of transportation, the price of staple food pro-1 ducts, especially of cereals, is much the same the world over, aud the recent increase in price has been the result of a world-wide cause. But a source of supply as near as Canada would certainly help to prevent speculative fluctuations, would steady local price movements, and would postpone the effect of a further world increase in the price of leading commodities entering into the cost of living, if that be inevitable.

In other words, agreeing with Mr. Hill and agreeing with all people wbo have studied this question, the President recognizes that as both Canada and the United States have a surplus of wheat the price must be ruled by the price at Liverpool, and it is just as idle as anything possibly can be ; it is not appealing to the intelligence of the people of Canada, to argue that there will be any substantial or permanent increase of price by reason of this reciprocity arrangement. My hon. friend argued though that the United States would soon cease to be a country producing a surplus of grain. The hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) tells us that there will be immediately an enormous increase in the production of grain in Canada by reason of this reciprocity and that reciprocity is going to be mutually beneficial. With the vast areas available for producing wheat in the United States, and -with an enormously increased production there, is it not idle for my hon. friend to talk about getting an advantage by reason of that feature of the argument? Mv hon. friend says that if we had a million more people in the west what a great stimulus it would be to the industry of Ontario. Yes, it would be if we were getting their trade. He says that Mr. LENNOX

the manufactured productions of his own city, and probably of Ontario generally, go to the west. Yes, they go to the west, but they go on the basis of exchange. Will that continue if the products of the west are poured down into the United States? My hon. friend says : How can you expect :ha""t manufactured goods will come into Canada? They will come into Canada because of a law which has been in existence for a long time that where you will sell you will buy, and the return cargo is something which enters very largely into the question, of the price. They will carry grain, cattle and other products of the west down into the various states of the union, they will have a cargo and what more natural than that we should deal very largely with people to whom we have sold. I notice that the hon. member for South Wellington is quite convinced on this subject- when he became convinced I do not know-but he is perfectly convinced-that this proposal is all right, and that Canada as a whole is going to gain by it. I admit he did not show us how but he said that Canada is going to gain. How long has my bon. friend been of that opinion? I remember that a little while ago a prominent gentleman from the Senate, Sir George W. Ross, made a very eloquent address before the Board of Trade in Toronto. He demonstrated as clearly as a proposition can be demonstrated that reciprocity would be prejudicial to the interests of Canada. He demonstrated that and he pronounced his opinion very distinctly at a time when reciprocity of a much more confined character was supposed to be what was in contemplation than what it has turned out to be. I have to ask my hon. friend from South Wellington if it is a fact that he wrote Sir George W. Ross approving of his attitude, or of the address he made upon that occasion, and congratulated him?

Applying ourselves to the question of material prosperity, how will this affect the country ? I have referred to the question of grain, but theTe is another feature of it, that if a large quantity of our gfain goe3 to the United States without being converted into a more finished product such as flour, meal, food cereals and the like we will be losing all the advantage that results from the by-products, and that is a very important question in mixed husbandry such as we will have to practise in Canada. There is one feature of this tariff that I think will be invoked as being a source of profit to the farmers, that is hay. What

effect that will have in places where the farmer lives near the border, I am not prepared to say, I do not think it will have very much. It is not a question of course, of what the tariff is, but of what the prices are in the two countries, and if we do not want to ship hay into the United States, it matters not at all what the tariff may be. But having some practical knowledge on this question, as I always profess to have on agricultural questions, I would say he is rather a poor class of farmer who aims at selling his hay. The wise farmer, the progressive farmer, will not generally sell hay, he will convert it into the finished product by feeding and fattening his stock and thus getting an additional advantage. Further, he restores to the soil the fertility and the productiveness that has been taken temporarily from it in the production of this hay. So a wise farmer will not avail himself to any extent of this opportunity, and I would deplore it very much if any large quantity of our hay should go across the boundary line, because I feel it would be almost equivalent to transferring the fertility of our farms to the United States. Thus, after giving the Americans command of our fruit growing industry, we would be furnishing them with means to build up more and more -their fruit industry and proportionately impoverishing that industry in our country. Let me now call your attention to the message of the President of the United States to his government. The dominant note in that message is warning: That the Dominion of Canada has greatly prospered, that it has an active, aggressive and independent people, that ' they have come to the parting of the ways,' that the United States have repelled those people for 40 years, that the 'Canadians had been

looking to the United States for years for the development in their trade but had now turned their faces away from that country to Great Britain, that the United States had gone too far, and would have to act now promptly or Canada would escape altogether. Another note of warning in the president's message is this: We have wasted our natural resources, we have overrun half a continent, there is a rich half continent to the north of us in the possession of the Canadians, we need to be active now to take the opportunity of overrunning that other half. The Canadian people, he says, have now a definite self-Teliant, safe policy, a policy which they have implemented by a magnificent transportation system, and which is calculated to work in harmony with the interests of Great Britain, and therefore now is the time for the United States to act. The tables are turned on us, says President Taft, the Canadians have taken stock, they are guarding their pulpwood and at any moment they may take means to safeguard their forests and mines and fisheries, so that we shall be cut out from these permanently unless we act without delay. How shall we meet them? We must meet them in the bond or semblance of friendship before their policy becomes too crystallized and fixed for change. That is the statement summarized of the President of the United States to his'people. Well, I have a dominant note which I would like to put into my address to you this afternoon. I say also that we are at the parting of the ways, that this is a momentous crisis in the affairs of Canada and Britain. It is the most momentous crisis since the Boer war. What should we do? My reply is this: Stand firm by the policy which has made Canada, build up our own ocean ports, increase transportation, multiply and stimulate the avenues of communication, strengthen our interprovincial bonds, promote interprovincial trade, unite all Canada in cpmmerce, in interest, in sympathy and in aspiration, foster the sentiment of Britisr-Canadian nationality, preserve at all hazards our British connections, and steadily and strenuously strive for imperial preferential trade.

I desire to trace a little further the reason for this offer from the United States. If we look into the causes we will probably be able to ascertain the motives at work. There were three important events occur-ing about 1893. There was the Chamberlain propaganda at the time, the idea of creating a closer bond of trade between the various parts of the British Empire. It had its beginning earlier, but taking definite form about 1893, it began to attract attention then. Then we had the launching of the National Transcontinental railway scheme. These two matters together had a very marked influence upon the opinion in the United States. Why? Because of the declarations made at that time by the right hon. gentleman who leads this House. It is true that before then there had been on our statute-books an offer of reciprocity. At that time the American papers began to say that reciprocity with Canada would be a good thing. And why? Because they realiz-Mr. LENNOX.

ed that they were losing their opportunity; they realized that there was a likelihood that a closer bond of union between the empire and Canada would be effected, and that if imperial preferential trade was ever accomplished, then goodbye to the chance of the United States having closer union with the Dominion of Canada. 330455,ca.proc.d.1911-02-16.3.2.62,1911-02-16,5bfd2fe5-bfe6-42c4-9503-71c3b6f865df,ca.m.5370,Mr. LENNOX.,,WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH UNITED STATES.,,,I would like to conclude before six o'clock. To continue the extract from Mr. Sherman's speech.

The settlement of the northwest territory, the Louisiana and Florida purchases, the annexation of Texas, and the acquisition from Mexico are examples of the adaptation of our form of government for expansion, to absorb and unite, to enrich and build up, to ingrafc in our body politic adjacent countries, and while strengthening the older states, confer prosperity and development on the new states admitted into this brotherhood of republican states. . . . With a firm conviction that this consummation most devoutly to be wished is within the womb of destiny, and believing that it is our duty to hasten its coming, I am not willing, for one, to vote for any measure not demanded by national honour that will tend to postpone the good time coming, when the American flag will be the signal and sign of the union of all the English-speaking peoples of the continent from the Rio Grande to the Arctic Ocean.
And running through a recent editorial in the New York * American,' I find the following:

On the opening day of the British parliament the Conservative leaders of both Lords and Commons forgot for the moment their critical and distressing domestic difficulties and uttered a loud cry of protest against trade reciprocity between Canada and the United States. Lord Lansdowne exclaimed in the House of Lords: The whole history of the British Empire will be changed if the great Dominion is encouraged, by agreement with the United States, to develop itself not on imperial lines but in accordance with geographical conditions.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Haughton Lennox,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=5bfd2fe5-bfe6-42c4-9503-71c3b6f865df&Language=E&Section=ALL

Let Congress pass the Canadian reciprocity Bill and all the plans of the English reactionaries for killing American trade will crumble to the ground.

In ratifying this trade agreement we should understand therefore that we are settling a world problem, and settling it right. British imperialism will wane in consequence, but American trade routes will run along the lines that were ordained by nature.

When all is said the natural interchange between the United States and Canada is of immense scope, in spite of all artificial barriers. It will be something prodigious-like the sweep of tides-when a new reciprocity agreement shall breach the tariff walls and
ive disappointed nature half a chance to have
er way.

330458,ca.proc.d.1911-02-16.3.2.65,1911-02-16,5bfd2fe5-bfe6-42c4-9503-71c3b6f865df,ca.m.5370,Mr. LENNOX.,,WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH UNITED STATES.,,,So, they say it was all a joke. Let me read exactly what he said, and the country can judge whether it was a joke or not:

Washington, D.C., February 15.-During the debate in the House yesterday on the Canadian reciprocity Bill, Congressman James Beauchamp Clark, the man who will be next speaker of the House of Representatives and whose party will be the majority in the next House, made this reference to the Bill.
Now comes what Congressman Clark said:

' X am for it, because I hope to see the day when the American flag will float over every square foot of the British North American possessions clear to the north pole. They are people of our blood. They speak our language. Their institutions are much like ours. They are trained in the different art of self government. My judgment is that if the treaty of 1854 had never been abrogated, the chances of a consolidation of these two countries would have been much greater than they are now.

I do not have any doubt whatever, that the day is not far distant when Great Britain will see all of her North American possessions become a part of this Republic. That is the way things are tending now.

Having said that much, I want to say another thing. I do not confine my support of reciprocity bills to this one. I am in favour of reciprocity treaties with the Central and South American republics, including Mexico.
The intelligent farmers of America know

that the agricultural products of Canada are inconsiderable when compared with the agricultural products of the United States. To use a common phrase, they do not constitute a drop in the bucket. They also know that wages are as high in Canada in many lines as in America, and higher in labour pertaining to the production of lumber, so they know too- much to be scared by the overworked cry of ' pauper labour.'

Mr. Norris-' I wanted to ask the gentleman (Mr. Clark) something along the line of universal peace. As I understand it, the gentleman favours this Bill, for at least one reason, that it will have tendency in the end to bring Canada into the Union? '
Mr. Clark, of Missouri-' Yes, sir; have no doubt about that.'
Mr. Norris-' Will that have a tendency to preserve peace with Great Britain? '

Mr. Clark, of Missouri-* Why, certainly it will. I do not have any doubt whatever that the day is not far distant when Great Britain wil joyfully see all of her North American possessions become a part of this Republic.
That is the way things are tending now.'
Mr. Martin, of South Dakota-' Will the gentleman favour the abrogation of our tariff law entirely so far as Canada is concerned and making free trade with Canada on all products?'
Mr. Clark, of Missouri-' By taking Canada in to become a part of the United States. Yes.'
That is pretty clear language.

330461,ca.proc.d.1911-02-16.3.2.68,1911-02-16,d48d6401-4298-4675-800a-0bb113070c33,ca.m.4070,Mr. A. B. WARBURTON (Queens, P.E. I ).",,WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH UNITED STATES.,,,"Mr. Chairman, I listened with great interest to the speech of my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) in which he outlined and defined the policy of his party not only along the lines which were taken by his leader and others, but on other lines as well, elaborating even to a somewhat greater extent than they did. I do not propose to discuss directly the remarks of the hon. gentleman at any great length, because a good many of the subjects that he touched upon-and touched upon so well-I propose to take up in the

course of the remarks I had outlined for myself before he spoke. But I would like for a moment, to touch upon one or two of the points to which he referred. I do not say that in all cases I take exception to what he said, because he often says things with which I agree, but, often' says things to which I cannot personally assent. As to the subject of a tariff commission, which the hon. gentleman brought up, I go so far as to say that the question is one that might well be discussed. I cannot say, however, that I personally agree with the idea of such a tariff commission as the hon. gentleman evidently had in mind. If you like to appoint a number of experts with whom the government or any one else can consult on tariff questions, well and good. But that course, I take it, the government can follow for tjhemselvesi; the'y do not need any recommendations or any legislation to that end. No doubt, every minister takes good care, and especially, perhaps, the Finance Minister, to consult with experts on subjects with which he has to deal. But to appoint a tariff commission such as I understand to be proposed by the hon. member (Mr. Lennox), would be, I think, as has been said in this House, in effect, to alter the position of ministers as responsible advisers of thejlrown; it would be more or less an abrogation of the principles of responsible government. I can quite understand that the Manufacturers.' Association, that body of able, influential and talented business men, would like to have a tariff commission, particularly as it would be almost certain that that commission would be largely, if not entirely, composed of those who would, perhaps, be recommended by that association. Whether the great mass of the consumers, the farmers, would have an equal voice in such a commission I think open to question. When the people of this country send something over two hundred members to this House, and when, at the head of this House is a government responsible to tne House, and to the people for what they do, I do not think it would be well to relieve the government or this House of the responsibility which they were sent here to assume.

Now, we are told ' let well enough alone.' That is a very good saying m its way, but, as has been pointed out before, it does not go quite far enough. Had we ' let well enough alone ' in the past, there would have been no progress. This country must move on. In this I am only repeating what has been said before, but this idea of leaving well enough alone has been so pressed upon this House, and, by the press of the country, upon the people, that I think I am justified in returning to it. The Anglo-Saxon race is incapable of standing still. The French Canadian race and the various other nationalities which go to make up the Canadian people, and which will eventually

be fused into one race in this country, are incapable of standing still. If they tried to stand still, they would soon deteriorate, and then Canada would become a country that would be fit to be annexed to some other, because it would be unfit to take care of itself. The hon. member for South Sim-coe (Mr. Lennox) announced somewhat oracularly that he hoped the common sense of parliament would not allow this Bill to go through. I shall have to plead guilty to great lack of common sense, if the hon. gentleman is right in assuming that common sense would be against this Bill; because my feeling has been and is to support this Bill to the utmost of my ability. And, in so doing, I know that I shall have the almost unanimous support of my constituency; and if, to-morrow, I had to run an election I would want no other question than this upon which to go before the electors. I trust the hon. member for South Simeoe (Mr. Lennox) , in that oracular deliverance of his, did not arrogate to himself the right to say that there is no common sense to be found outside those holding the views that commend themselves to his judgment. I hold that there is common sense on both sides of the House; that neither side has the monopoly of common sense, though it is a much rarer thing than its name would imply.

One exception taken to the agreement was that, the United States and Britain, having been placed on a parity so far as concerns the admission of their manufacture into this country, Great Britain would be really placed in a worse position because of the long haul she has. There might be some small ground for that argument, but really the matter is so small that, when you remember that Great Britain has practically the carrying trade of the world and carries all the products in her own bottoms, and that this is mainly water carriage, which is the cheapest carriage there is, it is questionable whether the cost of bringing goods from Great Britain to Canada would be much, if at all, greater than the cost of bringing them across, for instance, from New York to Toronto. I know that, as a matter of practice, it costs more to bring English goods from Halifax to Charlottetown, than it costs to bring them from Liverpool to Halifax. That is one of the perennial subjects of complaint with us-that we pay so much for rail carriage when water carriage is so cheap.

In dealing with the various articles which have been made free, the hon. member for South Simeoe (Mr. Lennox) referred to the article of hay. To a great extent, I agree with the remarks which the hon. gentleman made in regard to the way farmers should treat their hay. But as to the way farmers put up their hay or as to the way they dispose of it, that is a maiter the government cannot very well control. It is only Mr. WARBURTON.

on the commercial side that the government and parliament can deal with it. I agree that the best course for the farmers to take with their hay, under ordinary conditions, would be to feed it. But it sometimes happens that there is a superabundance of hay. That is what happened in Prince Edward Island last year. While- we had really a failure in what is usually our best staple crop, potatoes, the hay crop was fifty per cent higher than it had ever been before-an enormous crop. We cannot feed it, because we have so much more hay than the stock we have can use. There is no use sending it to Quebec or any of the other provinces, because they have plenty of hay. We have been shipping a little to England, but that is a long and difficult matter. If the hay is allowed to go into the United States markets in the spring, I think we ought to be able to do a good business with our surplus hay. And that is the best thing to do with it, as it cannot stay there forever, and we have not sufficient live stock to use it. But, even if the farmers do not adopt the scientific method of farming and feed their hay, working it up into the finished product of beef, why should we say to them:
column2: You

column1: have to do as we tell you to do; you must feed when we tell you to, and you must not ship until we tell you to? This is a free country, and we must leave them some judgment as to how they shall treat these matters on their own farms.

But, that is not the matter that affects this agreement most. The point is raised that the agreement will be apt to divert trade from the lines running east and west to the lines running north and south. I have not many fears on that score. I listened to the wail when the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lennox) tried to convince us that there was now no need for the Transcontinental railway, no need for the Hudson Bay railway, no neea for the Georgian Bay canal or the deepening of the Welland canal. Individually, it would not affect me very much whether these public works were built or not, but as a Canadian it affects me very closely, and I desire to look at the question from the general standpoint of Canada. For that reason, though these things are no direct advantage to us, I believe they should be undertaken, and I do not think the agreement will militate against the completion of these enterprises. When this agreement comes into operation, the chances of these works being soon built will be greatly improved. With the great fertility of our soil, with Canada's enormous production in minerals, in lumber, and in the fruits of the field, I have no_ doubt whatever, but that our population is sure to increase, and, in a few years, we shall be able to provide traffic for all these roads whether they run north and south or east and west.

Not only that, 'but I believe the time is coming shortly when we will have to increase the number of our railroads, not only north and south, but also east and west. It may be that I am unduly optimistic, nevertheless I have a firm and abiding faith in the future of Canada, in our producing powers, and in the energy and ability of our peo;ple. I believe as firmly as I believe I am speaking to you, Mr. Chairman, that the superabundance of the produce of Canada of all kinds will afford ampler employment for all these roads and canals, and you will even have to multiply them. The opposition of our Conservative friends is in line with the course that they have been pursuing for many years. I do not know whether it has become second nature to them to look upon every move that is undertaken as an indication of coming blue ruin, but certainly whenever a proposition is made to improve the condition of our people, if it means any advantage worth talking about, their course leads us to believe that they have no hope whatever for Canada, that they are pessimistic, even ultra-pessimistic, and that if we were to believe all they say we had better pack up and get out of Canada for some other country. I do not believe that this agreement is going to affect our credit in Great Britain adversely. When we see that since this agreement has been made public the stock of our greatest railway company, and the one most likely to be affected, the Canadian Pacific railway, has gone up several points within the last 48 hours, we must recognize that the shrewd men who manage that road have no fears of the effect of this agreement upon the money market, or upon the condition of affairs in this country. They have no fear that their great road is going to become a streak of rust for want of traffic. I saw, the other day, a statement from Sir Donald Mann, who ought to know something about railroads, that this agreement was not going to affect adversely his road. Now, I would take the opinion of Sir Donald Mann, aided by what little common sense I may happen to possess, to be that this agreement, instead of being likely to harm his road, is much more likely to do it good. Then there is the loyalty cry. Whenever a matter affecting the tariff or the position of Canada is brought up, we always expect to hear the loyalty cry raised, and I propose to discuss it at some length later on. Just here, however, I will say one or two words. My hon. friend points out to us that we should strive for imperial preference and preferential trade. Well, that is a nice thing, a pleasing thing to listen to; but within the last three or four years imperial preferential trade has been beaten out of its boots in Great Britain itself. Not long ago, in 1906, when the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) went to Great Britain to stump the country in favour of preferential trade within the empire, preferential trade was defeated in the new House of Commons by a majority of something over 300, and the member for North . Toronto did not deem it advisable to stay there long, because he was not making much impression. Again, a little over a year ago, in January or February last, the matter was again brought before the people of Great Britain, and again it was defeated in the new parliament by a majority of something like 120. Only the other, day it came up again, along with other matters, when the leaders of the Tariff Reform party looked upon it as such an absolutely hopeless proposition that in his great speech in the Albert .hall Mr. Balfour was obliged to throw it overboard, and to say that now all they were asking for was a referendum, in order to get their own followers into line. This shows that the big men of the party in Great Britain have lost confidence in the. cry of preferential trade. Of course, if the people of Great Britain should offer us a preference in their markets we would be only too glad to take it, but that is a matter for them to decide, not for us, and already they have spoken very clearly and have said that they would have none of it.

We are just now hearing a good deal about the foolish remark made by Mr. Champ Clark the other day in the United States Congress. Well, we must always expect talk of that kind on the other side of the line; we have lots of it here, and we cannot expect that our people should indulge in talk about annexation, and this, that, and the other thing, impugning the loyalty of their opponents, and trying to make out that our lot is ultimately to be cast in with the great republic-I say we cannot expect to have a monopoly of that sort of foolish talk; it must spread to the other side of the line, they are men like ourselves, pretty much the same blood as ourselves, and they will talk. But I will tell you how it appears to me in reading newspaper extracts from time to time. It appears to me that a great part, I won't say all, of this filbustering talk in the United States has been manufactured for the purpose of defeating the Bill there, pretty much as I believe a great deal of the talk of a like character has been manufactured on this side of the line-I won't say all of it in the House of Commons-for the same purpose. If you find our own press throughout the country, or a large part of it- because there are noble exceptions on the Conservative side-if you find large and influential portions of our press taking the ground that this is going to lead to annexation, you can scarcely expect that it. will not have some effect on our American friends, and that they will not think that perhaps there is something in it. But they

do not recognize as clearly as we do that it is simply a piece of political manoeuver-ing, and that it is of small importance, as we know it to be. We also see a statement in the papers the last day or two that the right hon. the Prime minister went into this undertaking in concert with the government of Great Britain and President Taft; in other words, that the only meaning to he derived from this agreement is that the government of Canada, with the Prime Minister at its head, the Premier of Great Britain, and the President of the United States, have ioined in a foul conspiracy in order to detach Canada from the British Crown, and to add it to the territories of Uncle Sam. I think, Mr. Chairman, that the mere statement of an agree-men such as that carries with it its own refutation. The idea of the Prime Minister of the British Empire intriguing with the head of a foreign state, and with the head of the greatest of the over-sea nations of the empire, to bring about a dismemberment of that empire, carries its own refutation with it, and I do not think it requires to be referred to at any greater length. I see in this morning's paper a telegram by the Canadian Press cable, an extract from a speech of Mr. Asquith, which I will read:

London, Feb. 15.-The A me r i c a n-C an a d i a n reciprocity agreement came to the fore in the House of Commons again to-day. The government was questioned regarding the statement attributed to Henri Bourassa, Nationalist leader in the legislature of Quebec, to the effect that the home government had encouraged the Canadian government to conclude a reciprocity trade understanding with the United States.
Premier Asquith replied: ' The statement is entirely without foundation in fact.' The premier also denied that Ambassador Bryce has been engaged actively in the process to bring about the agreement.
Now, Sir, I would again point out, as it cannot be too often pointed out, that off and on for forty or fifty years past, some form of reciprocity has been advocated by both parties in Canada.

They have differed from time to time as to the method by which that policy should be carried out but it was recognized until recent years by this country and this parliament as the policy of one party as well as the other. In 1891 'Sir John Macdonald made his last appeal to the electors of Canada, and he appealed to them on this very question. Although the language used by him on that occasion has been quoted more than once, as it is necessary in order to connect what I wish to say, I propose to read it again. He said in his manifesto to the people of Canada :
We said to the Americans we are perfectly willing to trade with you on equal terms. We are desirous of having a fair reciprocity Mr. WARBURTON.
treaty; but we will not consent to open our markets to you while yours remains closed to us.

That was a very laudable position to take. That was the position I would expect Sir John Macdonald to take. He was an astute statesman. I was not a follower or a supporter of his, tout I always recognized his great ability.
