330466,ca.proc.d.1911-02-16.3.2.73,1911-02-16,d48d6401-4298-4675-800a-0bb113070c33,ca.m.4070,Mr. WARBTJRTON.,,WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH UNITED STATES.,,,I submit it with all its infirmities and imperfections, and, while it may be bad poetry, it gives a very clear idea of what would happen if the British preference fell into the hands of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster). Then, for fear the cry of the British preference would not be enough, hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House have-on this, as on many other occasions, raised the cry of loyalty. During the course of my career as a public man in Canada, I can recall no occasion of this kind when an important public measure was advanced by the Liberal government, that the cry of loyalty was not raised by our opponents. Indeed, so often has it been raised that like the cry of ' wolf, wolf,' the people of Canada pay very little attention to it. At best it is an absurd cry. The loyalty of Canadians, whether they be Liberals or Tories, is too robust to be destroyed by any question of our trade relations with the United States. I do not think that any man can honestly and sincerely say that he believes in his heart of hearts that a single Canadian citizen will have his loyalty impinged in the slightest degree because we have freer trade relations with the United States or with any other country.

If it were not that I personally know so many of the hon. gentlemen on the opposition side of the House, and so many of their supporters throughout the country I would almost feel that they had lost confidence and belief in the robustness and virility of their own race, I would feel that they had almost lost confidence in their own loyality; but knowing them as I do, knowing them to be as loyal as we are, no more and no less, I feel that they are doing themselves a great injustice when they put before this country for political effect this matter of a possible want of loyalty. It is unworthy of them, unworthy of men of their class. If we were a lot of hoodlums or if we were to be bought and sold perhaps they might be justified in taking that ground, but if we were that class of people it would not matter much what country we belonged to. But we do not belong to that class of people, the people of this country are of an entirely different class. Nor do the people of this country think, as our hon. friends seem to think, that everything is going to the bad. Still, if one wrere to judge by their uttered words,

he would almost be inclined to think so. Sometimes when I hear these hon. gentlemen talking of loyalty and annexation, that we are going to be annihilated as a nation, and I do not know what else, I look around; I see that if you take their words literally these men have lost faith in their country and I am inclined to say : Oh ye of little faith. I believe, however, that they have a better faith than that, that their belief in the country is strong and robust and that when we get this reciprocity agreement fairly under way we will find among them among the strongest of its true and loyal supporters.

I used to belong to a vestry where we had one fine old gentleman who opposed everything proposed, no matter what it was. He was a very fine old man, and a generous supporter of the church, and when we got to know him we simply let him talk a little and then went ahead with what was proposed in spite of his opposition. When he had opposed whatever was suggested, he felt he had done his full duty, and always supported what we had done by his money and his efforts, and if you wished to repeal next week, what he had opposed last week, he would oppose the repeal. Just so with our opposition friends and the British preference. If you attempted to repeal the British preference now' there would be as strenuous an opposition from the hon. gentlemen as there was to its enactment. One of the evils of the protective system, and I have no belief in protection myself and never had, is that it has the effect of destroying a man's self-reliance, he will rely more on the assistance of a high protective tariff than on his own exertions. I would like to test the loyalty of the hon. gentlemen in another W'ay, and I hope and trust the government will see their way to make the test, although I do not know that they have any intention of doing so. I would like to see the British preference increased to 50 per cent, and I for one will assure them of my strong support; I will work for it, and do the best I can for it, I will hail it as a further and greater exhibition of our loyalty, and I am sure from what we have heard since the discussion here that hon. gentlemen opposite will support the government with both hands in anything of that kind.

WARBURTON.,,WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH UNITED STATES.,,,And I would be very much interested, I w'ould not leave my seat for one moment when that matter came up, as I would love to listen to the cries of loyalty that would then be uttered by them.

Turning to the question of annexation, I would say and I have no doubt I speak for many others here that it is humiliating for a loyal subject of the empire, such as I am, to be placed in a position where it is

necessary to defend any section of this country or to have to denounce even the suspicion that this great country of ours has the slightest inclination or intention or could be induced to go into annexation. I believe there is a way, by a long course of treatment, in which you might force this country to go in for independence, but never for annexation. I do not want to see either independence or annexation, I think we are remarkably well off where we are. But we had talk about reciprocity many years ago. Conditions and times may change, but the effect of similar principles is always the same although conditions may divert them somewhat. Before 1854 it was notorious that there was an annexationist sentiment in this country. I do not think it got down to the maritime provinces, but there certainly was such a sentiment in the present provinces of Quebec and Ontario. That sentiment was voiced by a number of very able men, and I think they were not confined to one side of politics-although some one said yesterday that they were all Conservatives-young men and very able men, of whom a remarkable number on both sides of politics later came very much into the limelight and rendered good service to their Queen and to their country. After a few years of weakness when they entertained annexationist sentiments-it was the hot blood of youth, I fancy more than anything else, they perhaps were benefited by having gone through the annexation fever just as patients are sometimes better after suffering from certain fevers- they held high place in the councils of this country, and their names to-day are deservedly held in honour as those of loyal, manly subjects of the British Empire, none more loyal than they. I read in this pamphlet opposing reciprocity that was sent to me a very good summary of the history of that annexation sentiment. If we are to believe what we are told of that period, that annexation sentiment was stopped by reciprocity. I quote:
Though reciprocity Bills had been defeated in Congress in 1848 and 1849, it was seen by the southern representatives.
And here is how we came to get it. .

That the idea was not only favoured by Great Britain and Canada, but was gaining ground in all the northern states, and, when the agitation for annexation began to develop, leaders of opinion in the South took quiet note of it, and foresaw that the alternative to a reciprocity treaty might be a complete union of the Canadian provinces with 'the States, in which case the separatist movement in the southern States would be swamped by a new union element in the North. Then the southern senators yielded and withdrew their opposition to the treaty, and thus in the decree of Providence, the motive which determined the southern States to secede, and which brought on ithe terrible civil war,

gave to Canada her desires without the sacrifice of her British connection, and, the economic waste of the same war bringing up at its close new revenue problems, cut Canada off from her dependence on the trade of the States, and thus confirmed her against her wishes, in the path of a separate existence as a nation.
Again the same writer, at page 13, says:

In the northern States political opposition to reciprocity yielded partly to the pressure of commercial needs on both sides, and partly to the belief that the new commercial relationship would lead to political union. The south, believing with most Canadians that reciprocity alone would satisfy the provinces, favoured the treaty to keep them out of the union, fearing their influence on the secession movement. The intuition of the south was correct, for, as soon as the treaty was negotiated, the annexation sentiment, which was never very deep, died out.
I would like also, although it has often been quoted before, to read you an extract from Joe Howe's speech at Detroit. It cannot be quoted too often in Canada:

In my own family and person I have suffered not a little by this unhappy rebellion. I have five hoys, and one of them took it into his head to enter your army. He has now been nearly two years in the 23rd Ohio Regiment, and has fought in all^ the battles of that regiment during this period. He was in both the great battles under Sheridan, in which General Early's forces were scattered and the Shenandoah valley cleared. All the personal benefit that I have derived from the reciprocity treaty or hope to derive from its renewal, will never compensate me or that boy's mother for the anxiety we have had with regard to him: but when he produced his certificate of his commanding officer, showing that he had conducted himself like a gentleman and had been faithful and brave, it was some consolation for all our anguish to know that he had performed his duty. (Enthusiastic applause. As the applause subsided a gentleman proposed 'Three cheers for the boy,' which were given with great heartiness.) I have heard it said since I came to the convention that if the reciprocity treaty is annulled the British provinces will be so cramped that they will be compelled to seek annexation to the United States. I know the feeling in the lower provinces, and I believe I am well enough acquainted with the Canadians to speak for them also when I make the assertion that no considerations of finance, no question of balance for or against them on the interchange of commodities can have any influence upon the loyalty of the inhabitants of the British provinces, or tend in the slightest degree to alienate the affections of the people from their country, their institution, their government and their Queen. There is not a man who dare, on the abrogation of the treaty, if such be its fate, to take the hustings and appeal to any constituency on annexation principles throughout the entire Dominion. The man who avowed such a sentiment would be scouted from society by his best friends. What other treatment would a man deserve wlio_ had turued traitor to liis government and violated for pecuniary ad-Mr. WARBURTON.

vantages all obligations to the country that gave him birth? The very boy to whom I have alluded as having fought manfully for the stars and stripes would rather blow his own father's brains out that haul dowh the honoured flag under which he was born. If any member of the convention harbours^ the idea that in refusing reciprocity to British America they would undermine the loyal feelings of the people of those colonies, he is
labouring under a delusion___I sincerely hope
that all thought of forcing annexation upon the people of Canada will be abandoned.

Mr. Howe's speech was throughout received in good spirit, and it is worth noting that at this convention a resolution was unanimously passed in favour of a reciprocity treaty between the two countries, and of extending its scope so as to include British Columbia, the Selkirk Settlement and Vancouver Island.

For my part I say 'Amen' to these words of that perh.apa one of our greatest Canadians. In that connection I would like also to read a short extract from a report in the ' Citizen,' a Conservative paper, which does not support the government in many things, but does, I am glad to say, in this matter:
The New York Sun declares that annexation is 'a dead issue,' and continues:-

The reciprocal trade relations of 1855-66 did not weaken the tie with the mother country. They set Canada up in business and gave her * confidence in her own resources. With their development that confidence has steadily grown.

And in reference to the situation as it exists to-day it is worthy of note that a condition parallel in almost every particular obtained over balf a century ago in our trade relations with the United States and Britain. But remarkable as it may appear in view of the interpretation placed upon such negotiations to-day, the modification of tariff duties was at that time considered the only possible salvation of Canada and the only method whereby annexation to the States could be prevented. In 1819 Lord Elgin, then Governor General, wrote that if Britain 'did not make the sacrifices which are absolutely necessary to put the colonists here in as good a position commercially as the citizens of the United
column2: States in
column4: freenavigation and reciprocal trade with the States
column7: mayhe nearer than we wot of.' And Lord Elgin followed this up some time afterwards with another communication in which he was even more outspoken. 'If/ he declared, 'things remain
column14: measure but the establishment of reciprocal trade between Canada and the United States or the imposition of a duty on the produce of the States when imported into England will remove it.'

column1: The reciprocity treaty of 1851, which resulted from Lord Elgin's representations, was followed by an almost complete cessation of annexation talk both in Canada and across the line. The fact became apparent then that the annexation spirit had had its origin in Canada in dissatisfaction with the commercial indifference of the mother country to her only North American colony, and that even

the slightest consideration in this respect was sufficient to dispel all such sentiment. Yet to-day we are told by political gospellers that the effort to promote friendlier trade relations with the United States is a menace to the imperial tie.

Now what took place before, may take place again. If there were any annexation sentiment in this country-and I have never seen the slightest sign of any-I believe the best cure for it would be freer trade relations. We are told by a very great authority Adam Smith:

That to prohibit a great people from making all they can of every part of their own produce, or from employing their own stock and industry in the way that they judge most advantageous for themselves, is a manifest violation of the most sacred rights of manhood.

This reciprocity agreement, which we are now discussing, is an effort made to allow the great mass of the people to make the best use of their own produce. It is to enable them to dispose of the produce of their fields and orchards, &c., to the best advantage absolutely in conformity with the principle laid down 100 years ago by Adam Smith and warmly approved of very recently by the most profound of modern historians Lord Acton. But, as I said a moment ago, there might be one possible way in which by a long continuance of a certain treatment our people might gradually be led to look for independence, although I am convinced they will never want annexation. Let me call attention to what was the real cause of the revolt of the North American colonies against Great Britain. We are so accustomed to hear about the Boston Tea Party that we perhaps do not often go as far back as the real origin of this trouble which caused a dissatisfaction in the New England colonies that grew until it became an overwhelming force and resulted in a severance of those colonies from the British Crown.

The real foundation of discontent which led to the American revolution was the effort of Great Britain, beginning in 1750, to regulate and control the occupation and business of the colonists. The final cause before the attempt to tax without representation was the effort to enforce the navigation law.

In other words, the effort to cramp and restrict the trade of these colonies was the underlying, the active, the effective cause of their separation from the motherland. Now, I do not think that even that would bring about annexation with the United States. I think we are too big a country; we have room enough for a nation. While we believe and hope and pray that we may ever remain a nation, one of the great congeries of nations which make up the British Empire, still, if, by any extraordinary concurrence of events, we should ever separate |

from Great Britain, it would be as an independent nation. We have a vast country; it is a northern country, and northern countries send out the best breed of men. And, if there is any other destiny open to Canada to which she is likely to attain, it would be independence and not annexation. And God forbid that it should be either.

But let us ask ourselves the question: Why should we join the United States? We here sit on opposite sides of this chamber -we do not know how long the parties will occupy their respective places; it may be fifteen or twenty years, perhaps only half-a-dozen years-but, though the sides oppose each other on the questions that come before us, I think we all agree that we have a much better form of government than the United States have. I do not think there is any dispute about that. Ours is a really responsible form of government. It can scarcely be said, if you examine it at all critically, that the United States government is really a responsible government. When you find that the members of the cabinet have not places on the floor either of the House of Representatives or of the Senate, that they are not directly responsible to the people, that when Congress changes its complexion the government still remains in office, it does not appear to me that that is, fairly speaking, responsible government at all. Ours is responsible government, and, on the whole, a better form. I believe, also, that we have a better country. In s-aying that I recognize the fact that we have a colder country, but the colder climate is the more bracing. We cannot raise the same great variety of products as can be raised in the United States, but those which we do raise are of the best, including men. I think we agree that we can raise in this country all that we really need. Even if we could have that country under the British flag, and if I were given my choice, I would not be willing to change countries. column1: So you see that Prince Edward Island, one of the most fertile parts of the Dominion. with fisheries surrounding it, suffered severely, our little manufactures were crushed out, and people left the country in considerable numbers. Nova Scotia, with
almost unlimited natural wealth, between the two last censuses only gained 9,000; and New Brunswick was in a .similar position.

Now I believe that this agreement, when it comes into effect, will do away to a large extent with the exodus from our provinces. I believe it will give our farmers better prices for their produce, and our fishermen better prices for their fish than they now get, and an improvement in those respects will tend to keep our young men ,at home on the farms. Much has been said in this House, and in the country as to the meaning of the balance of trade. I never had much confidence in the balance of trade theory, when I saw Great Britain, a free trade country, getting on so well, and Russia, a protectionist country, also showing a trade balance in its favour. During the last fiscal year we bought from the United States to the amount of $223,000,000, and they bought from us $113,000,000. Now that, as has already been pointed out, was largely due to the enormous quantity of raw material brought into this country for our manufacturers, and putting a number of articles on the free list. I think that the best way to encourage manufacturers is to put their raw material on the free list. But one reason especially why we have not sold a corresponding amount of goods to the United States, is owing to the high tariff that country has imposed upon our goods. We are accused of selling to our best customer, England, and of taking her money and spending it in the United States. There may be some truth in that, but it is not our fault, it is the fault of the high tariff in the United States.

I have said that we ought to look upon these matters rather from a broad and national point of view, than from a sectional or provincial point of view. I believe that every member of this House ought, as far as possible, to disassociate himself from all narrow views, and try to ascertain what will be for the greatest good of the greatest number in Canada, and I believe that that greatest good will be secured by the removal of these restrictions on trade with the United States. I have been informed by those who know, that while many farmers in the western provinces are becoming wealthy from the splendid crops they raise, there are many others, of whom we don't hear so much, who are heavily involved in debt, and have been obliged to mortgage their farms in order to find money to pay for the machinery they use. In this way the profit that they make upon their crops goes largely to pay the interest on loans. It is well known that the loan companies in Canada, and probably the same remark will apply to the United States, have large amounts invested in the west that have been taken by farmers. Now it takes the 118

farmer some ten or fifteen years to place himself in a good position, and as so much of his money has to go in payment of interest, he has an uphill Toad to pursue. He will get through all right if he is a man of vim and vigour, but he has got a terrible fight to put up in the meantime. Now I cannot see why, if these men, by selling their grain south of the line, can get a better price for it, they should not have the privilege of doing so. I for one, have a great deal of sympathy with the western farmer, who is struggling to make a start in life, and I say if he can get a few cents more for a bushel of wheat, it means a big relief for him, and will help him to get out of debt sooner. I think it is true that this agreement will bring about a relief to the consuming popiilation of Canada. It means a reduction of the tariff, perhaps not to a great extent. But to :my mind, a substantial reduction has already been made by the British preference, as well as by the treaties we have made with other nations, and the numerous articles put upon the free list. Still, with all these reductions, I am free to confess as an old Liberal, that I would like to see a still greater reduction in our tariff against foreign countries. To my mind, it does not render this agreement less valuable, because incidentally it takes in some other nations with which we have favoured nation treaties, I think it makes it so much the more valuable.

Now let us see what we give and what we get by this agreement. We place a considerable number of articles on the free list, and we reduce the duty upon a number of others, and the United States does the same for us. How do we come out from the point of view of revenue ? I will read an extract from the ' Citizen ' of the 9th inst, in which this matter is well put:
The ' Citizen ' says:

Tlie total production on Canadian products going into the United States is $4,849,933 under the terms of the new agreement. Of this sum the gain to Canada under Schedule A which wipes out all duties, is $4,236,988; under Schedule B, which admits articles to the United States at the same rate at which they enter Canada, the gain to this country's exporters is $234,984, while under Schedule C which calls for special rates, our gain is $377

In other words, the reciprocity agreement means in dollars and cents that Canada is getting the long end of a bargain, which will prove to the advantage of both countries concerned, to the extent of the difference between $4,849,930 and $2,363,763. Disregarding the advantages that must ensue for the consumer, the producer and the exporter the agreement is one that should appeal even to those who consider the financial aspect of such matters first and the effect upon the general prosperity of the country only when such an argument serves to support the original premise.
Nothing in the agreement would seem to",,,,

-justify the statements made in opposition to it that ' it will weaken the imperial tie ' or ' result in Canada's annexation by the United States.' In the last analysis these statements are reflections on the loyalty of the people of this country.

So that, in the matter of revenue, upon the articles placed on the free list, or upon *which the duty is reduced, we have made, it seems to me, a remarkably good bargain. I believe it is one that is good for both sides of the line. What are the articles which affect us particularly? The arrangement takes in all classes of cereals. We do not, in the maritime provinces, grow much wheat for export, but we grow other articles. We grow a sufficient quantity of wheat for our own use, or largely so, but we do not. pretend to be an exporting people in so far as wheat is concerned. Then we grow potatoes. Last year with us the potato crop was almost a failure. It is a very rare thing for it to be a failure in Prince Edward Island. It is usually our staple crop, but last year it was only half a crop, and I am not sure that it was even half a crop. There were produced last year in the maritime provinces:

The hay and clover in all these provinces was a remarkable crop. Turnips and roots were good, but potatoes were practically a failure. These potatoes were formerly shipped very largely to Boston by water, but the duty of 25 cents a bushel practically shut us out from the American market. We largely now supply Sydney, St. Pierre and Miquelon, Newfoundland, and some other places, but our natural market is Boston. While our shipments to the United States were at one time enormous, they have dwindled to very little. If that duty of 25 cents a bushel is taken off, is it conceivable that the shipment to our natural ports by water will not again be resumed and be as great a success as it formerly was, if not greater? If we can get that market for our potatoes and turnips it will add enormously to the wealth of our farms, and out farmers, as it is, are a pretty well off class.

Then again, we have fish. We scarcely realize the value of the fisheries of Canada. My hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury), occasionally brings up the question of the fisheries in the lakes of the west, and I myself, once in a while, say something about them, but I do not think that we realize the enormous value that our fisheries are to the country. We have had to contend with great difficulties owing to the fact that our fish- and this applies to all the maritime provinces-have been practically barred from the United States market by their duties. We have shipped largely to the West Indies, to South America, to Spain and to some of the ether European countries, which use large quantities of fish, but the near-by market Mr. WARBURTON.

we are, to a large extent, barred out from. If we get free entry of fish and fish oils into that near-by market it is inconceivable that a trade will not spring up as it formerly did, because we are right on the ground, transportation by water is cheap and there is an enormous demand for the fish that we put up-mackerel, for instance, and that sort of fish. Then, we raise a considerable

amount of poultry, which now we send very largely to Sydney, Newfoundland, and other places down there. We also produce dairy products. Up to now, we have sent these dairy products elsewhere than to the United States, although the United States would be our great market. We have been practically barred out from there. It happened by accident, in making up the schedules of the last tariff Bill of the United States, that they put cream in at five cents a gallon, although I believe the intention was to put it in at five cents a pound. Blit, however, it does go in at five cents a gallon, and already a large business in the exportation of cream has sprung up between Prince Edward Island and the United States. It began with only a few gallons, because people did not realize what it meant, but it has grown very largely and it will be a very important trade in another year. I hear that in Ontario the same thing has happened. Then again, we have large resources in live stock. We ship, as it is, large numbers of lambs to the United States. They come down and buy lambs in great quantities from us, because (Prince Edward Island lamb is noted for its peculiar excellence. But every lamb has to pay 75 cents, and every sheep, I believe, $1.50. Then we come to the question of fruit, which has been so much discussed by the hon. member for Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Burrell), and others. We have no dread whatever of the duty being taken off fruit. We are quite prepared to meet the Americans in their own market or anywhere else, we believe that the quality of our fruit will carry it anywhere. Our fruit comes in later in the season than the American fruit. Our strawberries are sent to the Boston market, after other supplies have failed, and we get a good market there. Our apples and pears are better than theirs, the flavour is better, and we are quite prepared to put our apples and our plums and such other fruit as we raise, in competition with theirs in any part of the world.

ARMSTRONG (East Lambton).,,WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH UNITED STATES.,CANNOT BOTH BE RIGHT.,,"Mr. Chairman, the question now before the committee is one of the most important that has been before parliament since confederation. The hon. member from the Garden of the Gulf has taken the position that he is very strongly in favour of reciprocity, and also of free trade with any nation on the face of the globe. But I venture to say that his good people, and the hon. gentleman himself, after he investigates this question more thoroughly will come to the conclusion, unless he and his people are taking a provincial view of the matter, considering only what is best from an island standpoint that we are facing a crisis in the affairs of this country. These people are big enough, and patriotic enough

and have sufficient national pride, I am sure, to say that even if they are going to get a few cents more for a bag of potatoes or some other commodity, and are thereby going to injure some of the other large industries in the different parts of this country, they would be willing to forego that slight advantage and work for the best interests of all.

My hon.-friend does not believe in a tariff commission. He says that 220 men are sent to this House to look after the tariff and should be able to do it. Well, what about the measure now before the House? Does he not know that it was submitted to us by two ministers of the Crown on behalf of the government, and that they are practically forcing their followers to line up and vote for it. Talk about 220 men having the right to decide this matter, I am not exaggerating when I say that every man on the government side is compelled to support this measure under penalty of seeing the government go down to defeat. This agreement is the work of two men, who are two of the strongest free traders and commercial unionists the country has ever known. Go back to the history of the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) and you will find him going up and down the highways and the byways of his province in the early days urging the people to secede from confederation and join their fortunes with the country to the south. And as to the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) we have heard him on the public platform throughout the cities of Ontario with that splendid voice of his crying aloud for free trade as it is in England. These are the two men who went to Washington and entered into a pact with the American people in order to bring about free trade between the two countries.

My hon. friend from Prince Edward Island (Mr. Warburton) says: Keep the hay on the farm. Yes, I would like to voice that sentiment. I would like to say to him that if he will get up in this House and condemn the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) for either his lack of knowledge or lack of interest in the agricultural industries of this Dominion during the last 15 years, owing to which our agricultural interests have been seriously interfered with, he will he doing something worthy of his election to parliament. If we had had a good, live, active Minister of Agriculture during the last 10 or 15 years, our farmers would not want to trade with the country to the south, but would be independent of any such necessity.

My hon. friend referred to the statement of Sir Donald Mann, which has also been referred to by other speakers on that side as supporting this agreement. The other day the hon. member for Wellington (Mr. COMMONS
Guthrie) read the whole of that statement. I propose to quote the last paragraph of it, which reads as follows :

Personally I would prefer to have a preference between the United Kingdom and the Dominion and between the Dominion and other colonies. This preference should be increased from time to time, until, say in 25 years, the cost of production would reach a common point throughout the empire. Then we would be able to have free trade within the empire, and protection against the nonBritish nations.

Does that statement indicate that Sir Donald Mann is strongly supporting the government on this question? I should say it indicates the very opposite, and that if he had his way he would take an entirely different course.

My hon. friend talks about a mutual preference, which, he says, would be a splendid thing for this country if it could be brought about. Let me go back to the days of 1896, just before this government came into office, and read what the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) said in London, Ontario, and again in Massey hall, Toronto, and a little latex I propose to read what the right hon. gentleman said at the Colonial Conference in old London. In London, Ontario, he said:

Now, the statesmen of Great Britain have thought that the governments of the colonies have come to a time when a new step can be taken in their development. What is that? That there should be a commercial agreement between England and the colonies. That practical statesman, Mr. Joseph Chamberlain, has come to the conclusion that the time has come when it is possible to have within the bounds of the empire a new step taken which will give to the colonies in England a preference for their products over the products of other nations.
He said further:

What would the possibilities of such a f-tep be if it were taken? We sell our goods in England; we send our wheat, our butter, our cheese, all our natural products, but there we have to compete with similar products from the United States, from Russia, and from other nations. Just see what an advantage it would be to Canada if the wheat, cheese and butter which we would send to England should be met in England with a preference over other products of other nations. The possibilities are immense. England does not expect that we should take her own system of free trade, such as she has it; but I lay it before you that the thing the English people would expect in return is that instead of the principle of protection, we should adopt a form of revenue tariff. Those are the conditions on which we could have that boom.
In closing he said:
My hope is-nay, my conviction is, that on the 23rd of June the Liberal party will be at the head of the polls. Then it will be the Mr. ARMSTRONG.
Liberal party, with its policy of revenue tariff, that will send commissioners to London to arrange for a basis of preferential trade.

Now, I would like to ask my good friend from the island (Mr. Warburton) what did the Prime Minister do? Did he send the commissioners over to old London? No one knows better than the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) what the Prime Minister said on this matter when he landed in Liverpool. In the first speech he made in that city on that question, the right hon. gentleman spoke as follows:

I claim for the present government of Canada that they have passed a resolution by which the products of Great Britain are admitted on the rate of their tariff at 12J per cent, next year at 25 per cent reduction. This we have done, not asking any compensation. There is a class of our fellow-citizens who ask that all such concessions should be made for a quid pro quo. The Canadian government has ignored all such sentiments. We have done it because we owe a debt of gratitude to Great Britain. We have done it because it is no intention of ours to disturb in any way the system of free trade, which has done so much for England. What we give by our tariff, we give you in gratitude for the splendid freedom under which we are prospering. It is a free gift. We ask no compensation. Protection has been the curse of Canada, and we would not wish you and we would not see you come under its baneful influence, for what weakens you must weaken us.
This speech no doubt won for the hon. gentleman the Cobden medal.

Follow up the ministers of the Crown from that day to this, follow up the men on the other side of the House, and what do you find ? You find the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher), fox instance, rising in his place and practically condemning the proposal of the men on this side, who were working for a mutual preference. Man after man on the other side has condemned in the strongest kind of ianguage the position that a mutual preference would be of benefit to the Dominion of Canada. We should have a mutual preference, and I firmly believe we will have it before many years go by. And, if it were not for this stumbling block of reciprocity, which these men put in the way, mutual preference would come all the sooner. Let me tell my hon. friend from Prince Edward Island (Mr. Warburton), that 48 per cent of the men who voted in the last general election in Great Britain, voted in favour of a mutual preference. It is idle to say that this idea is dead in the old country. It would increase the value of every farm in the Dominion, it would bring immigration to her shores that would fill our lands with a population worthy of our nation.
My hon. friend from Prince Edward Island talks about being a free trader, and

is anxious to take a step nearer to free trade. But I notice that the men who are such pronounced free traders, are not satisfied with the step; no sooner is one step taken than they want a further step. And what would free trade mean to the Dominion of Canada. One hundred and fifty millions of dollars per annum is collected for the purposes of this Dominion from our people. Assuming our population at 7,000,000, this means $20 per head or $100 per family. I only wish that, for a single year, the people of Canada had to put their hands into their pockets and pay out that $100 per family. They would watch where the money was going; and, instead of the government being allowed to squander, as they have been squandering, for the last fourteen years, the people would see to it that honest and clean administration was the rule in this country. My hon. friend wants free trade with the United States. That means that he is going to the most highly protected country in the world, and he is going there, because he can buy there cheap goods. He tells us about his potatoes. Why, what is he.going to gain by having access to the United States markets ? If he had read the Canadian reciprocity book, which has come to us from the Washington government, and printed by them, he would have found among the * articles included under the reciprocal trade agreement imported into the Dominion of Canada from the United States in the fiscal year ended, March 31,

the item of 215,288 bushels of potatoes valued at $179,000 and paying a duty of $43,000. (And the government, is doing away with that $43,000.) The hon. gentleman would have found that of sweet potatoes and yams we imported from the United States, 37,000 bushels, valued at $33,000. And before I get through, I will be able to show to my hon. friend that as to the farm products, which he is boasting of as being in so much demand among the people of the United States and of such increased value to the people of Canada by reason of this arrangement, the United States is net only a large exporter of these goods, but is not paying any extra price worth speaking of for any of them.

The hon. member referred to the British preference and told what a splendid thing it was for this country, but he did not take the figures into consideration. We imported from the United States within the past six years, $581,000,000 worth of goods, of which $502,000,000 were free goods. We imported from Great Britain during the same period $542,000,000 worth of goods, of which $113,000,000 were free goods. The rate on dutiable goods from Great Britain was 24 -78 as compared with 24 -26 per cent on dutiable goods from the United States; -and the rate or the total imports from Great Britain was

18 -64 per cent, while the rate on the total United States imports was only 13-4 per cent. Yet we hear these gentlemen boasting throughout the length -and breadth of Canada of the splendid advantages which, under this preference, they have granted to Great Britain. Our exports to the United States in the last six years amounted to $506,000,000, of which a large proportion was raw material, while -our exports to Great Britain amounted -to $726,000,000. During the past six years, Great Britain bought $300,000,000 worth more from us than we bought from her. During the same period, we bought from the United States, nearly $600,000,000 more than they bought from us. The British importer is paying higher duties to the revenue ' of the country than the man importing from the United States. Yet these gentlemen would lead us to believe that we are dealing with Great Britain to such a wonderful extent, and are, according to her many advantages.

My hon. friend (Mr. Warburton), spoke of annexation, and deplored the fact that the people of Canada were even discussing the subject. But when you take into consideration the prominent position that this great question holds- in the United States to-day, you cannot but feel that we should, at least take it into our serious consideration in this parliament. Hon. Ohamp Clark, the leader of a triumphant party, which swept the country in the United States elections last November, led his followers in the House of Representatives, in support of this reciprocity arrangement. Only three of his followers bolted this vote. He is the most prominent man in the Democratic party to-day. And we find that hon. gentleman making use of the words: ' We are preparing to annex Canada '- making use of them three times in his speech in the House of Representatives, on the -subject of this agreement. He said further, ' One flag, the Stars and Stripes, from Central America to the North Pole.' Amd we find prominent men in the United States backing him up in -this. I can give quotations from the statements of many prominent men in that country. I do not give many, because I do not wish to take up time. Senator Jones, of Washington, stated:
Canadian annexation is not an impossibility. It is remote, much as I would like to see Vancouver and British Columbia an integral part of the American Union.
Senator Smith of Michigan:

Champ Clark spoke in prophetic vein, and I am not surprised at his deductions. Mr. Clark's views, as expressed by him on the floor of the House on Tuesday, almost carry as much weight as if the Prime Minister of England had spoken. No doubt the jingoes in England will do all in their power to use the Clark incident to defeat the Canadian re-

ciprocity pact, if for no other purpose than the fact that reciprocity between Canada and the United States probably will shatter the well laid plans of England's statesmen to create a central parliament in London-a parliament that would make its purpose to secure advantage over trade relations between all countries flying the Union Jack and the world. Mr. Clark's utterances are bound to cause uneasiness in Europe, and are a blow at the English scheme of centralization, the feasibility of which is apparent to any one who studies the wonderful resources of the British Empire.
Can you imagine, Mr. Chairman, a stronger statement than that coming from one of the prominent senators of the United States? Then Senator Cummings, of Iowa, says:

I am for the annexation of Canada. I have always been, and if it were generally understood that Canadian annexation was the purpose of the pending pact, it doubtless would help the measure in becoming a law here. Mr. Clark's speech may have some effect on the outcome of the measure in England and' Canada, but surely not in this country.
Senator McCumber, of North Dakota:

Canadian annexation is the logical conclusion of reciprocity with Canada. Once the Canadian farmer has tasted the advantages of our market he won't want to withdraw. It would be a signal for a universal demand for annexation.

These quotations are from the utterances of leading statesmen at Washington. They undoubtedly voice the general idea in the United States with regard to this reciprocal agreement. Let me read a paragraph from a paper that serves a large district in western Ontario, the Detroit ' Free Press.' On February 2 it made this statement :

Its (the reciprocal agreement) principal merit is political and social. ... It will, it is hoped, and confidently hoped, be the beginning of the end of the stupid separation of two halves of a continent which is inhabited by substantially one people.
Then, what do we find President Taft of the United States saying at Champaign, Illinois:

What we ought to look toward is the general effect on the social and business relations of the two countries. We have no forts along onr borders; we have no battleships: we are able to live at amity with them. Why not then take down the only thing that separates us in our business relations?
Then at Springfield he said:
The plank in the platform of the last Re-publican convention, carried to its logical conclusion, would lead to substantial free trade with Canada.
He further said:
It will give the United States much greater control of the wheat market than it ever had before. It will enable its milling plants to Mr. ARMSTRONG.
turn Canadian wheat into flour and send abroad the finished product, and it will stimulate the sale of manufactures and other things that we have to sell in Canada.
Now let us inquire why the old treaty was abandoned:
The New York ' Sun ' reviews the causes which led to the cancelling by the United States of the reciprocity treaty of 1851, and says:

The treaty lasted about eleven years, dying of various causes on January 18, 1865. Among them was the charge that Canada in bad faith had raised her duties on manufactured goods (she has been acquitted by impartial commentators), a belief that Canada had the best of the bargain, the dissatisfaction of the American farmer and lumberman, and toward the end a general feeling of hostility toward England on account of her attitude toward the north during the civil war.

Can you imagine any arguments more trifling than those used for denouncing the reciprocity treaty in years gone by? And is it not possible that within the next few months, or the next few years, these same men may bring up like arguments when the Minister of Customs goes to change his tariff? He will find that the United States will hold the big stick over him as they did over the Finance Minister last year, when he had to withdraw from the position he had taken in reference to the. French treaty, when he led us to believe that the United States had no resource against the French treaty? He was told' on the floor of parliament that he wouldi have to yield to the United States, and he did yield by giving a number of concessions. Now you can depend upon it, that when you come to change your regular tariff from time to time, you will have to go over to Washington and consult with those men, and they will tell you plainly that they will withdraw from this reciprocity agreement unless you allow them certain privileges for their manufactured goods.

In a few weeks' time I believe the destiny of Canada will be fixed; we will either decide to be masters of our own future, or we will enter a path which can only lead to annexation. In 1866 Canada set her face towards welding together the British Empire. During all the years since, the United States has never held out her hand to help us, but on the contrary you find her building up against us a tariff wall forty-two rails high, while our wall is only twenty-six. To-day we are asked to take the first step towards turning aside from our beaten path. For fifty years we have gone on increasing in prosperity. Canada should have an ideal, and that ideal should be to become a great nation, while at the same time remaining a daughter in _ her mother's house. Everything a nation needs is produced in the

British Empire. Australia has the meat and the wool, Canada has the grain, thu raw material and the. lumber, Great Britain herself is the great manufacturing centre, and the clearing house of the world. Canada and Egypt can grow more and better cotton than the United States. Surely this is a world combination that cannot be beaten. To-day this government asks us to take the first step towards the disintegration of the empire. Does the government realize that the United States has precious few raw materials left compared with her needs? Let them go to the libraries in the United States and investigate the facts, and they will find that if the United States were compelled to use only her own pulpwood, in fifteen short years her supply of pulpwood would be consumed. Many of her coal mines and minerals have already struck rock bottom. Why is President Taft so anxious to carry out this agreement? Why is he going up and down that great country and gaining political prestige at every step? He realizes the need of prompt action on this agreement. He tells the people tjiat it will conserve their resources, it will open up new markets for their manufactures. He says Canada is at the- parting of the ways. Until the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Customs went to Washington, President Taft was politically a defeated man in the eyes of the people of the republic. To-day he can be elected easily on the ground that he was able to get this treaty from the hon. gentlemen; there is no question about it.

Why are the prominent men in the United States supporting this measure? Because they believe and know that they have the best of the bargain, and that it will lead to annexation. In so far as this reciprocity deal is concerned our representatives have been buncoed, and they have come back to this country with a gold brick. The premier's hands are tied with regard to this matter and the Minister of Customs has helped to tie his hands. The hon. gentleman knows full well that the hands of the Premier of Canada are tied and that he cannot change one jot or tittle of this important measure. We have the premier of this young Canada sitting in parliament with an important measure before him, his hands tied, and simply saying: In' so far as I am concerned I will not be able to change any part of it, and my followers will have to vote with me. Hands tied by whom, may I ask?-tied by the American diplomats, by the Yankee diplomats, by the men who got the Finance Minister and the Minister of Customs to go over there. After treating them no doubt in the most royal manner possible our representatives were invited in and finally, when the measure was placed before them, they thought it was of great advantage to Canada, no

doubt, owing to their free trade ideas, and they brought it back in the shape which it is presented to the House. No use for delegates to come to Ottawa! The Liberal press says to the manufacturer: Don't you grumble about the government's position on this question or they will hit you with the British preference. That position has been taken over and over again by the Liberal press. It is the same with the transportation companies-if you squeal your stock will be hit, and the important transportation companies of this country are in a most serious position, because should they condemn this measure, as they want to condemn it, and as they believe it ought to be condemned, that report will go abroad and it will be practically impossible for them to sell the stock of their railway or transportation companies. Canadians on this question like all others, ask for a square deal, but I cannot believe that this is a square deal. This government are the servants of the people, and not their masters. Instead of their bringing this measure down and forcing it through this House in the manner in which they are trying to force it through they should have given the people time to think over the matter and consider it properly. They must feel at least that they are taking an unfair advantage of the people in this regard.

We have had a great many treaty deals. We have had bungling mismanagement of our trade relations with many countries. When this government came into power in 1896 they granted a preference of 124 per cent to the mother land. When they granted that preference Sir Charles Tupper stood up on the floor of parliament and said distinctly and emphatically that they would have to grant the same concession to many other countries and Germany was one of those countries. But the Finance Minister said: No, we are not going to do anything of the kind. The outcome of it was that in 1898 he increased the preference to 25 per cent, and finally to 334 per cent. Germany said: You are hitting below the belt, you are taking an unfair advantage of us in reference to our position as a favoured nation in our treaty relations with the mother country-and rightly so. The outcome of it was that Germany put this country under the maximum tariff. This government turned around and put German goods under the maximum tariff. Germany said that this was another slap in the .face, and placed a surtax on our goods. Our government placed a surtax against German goods coming into Canada. The result was a tariff war and that tariff war was carried on year after year for twelve long years until the trade that we had with Germany which should have amounted to $50,000,000 a year had dwindled down to a paltry million or two. Who was the cause of

this trouble? This government. We find these hon. gentlemen coming down last year and removing that surtax, but not placing us back in the position that we were in in 1896. Our position with the German Empire is not anything like as favourable as it was in 1896. The Minister of Customs knows full well that in regard to many of the items they are not on the minimum tariff as they were in 1896. What about the German market? Germany with 62 million of people, Germany that imports two billions worth of goods, Germany that imports a billion worth of food products and 300 millions worth of just such products as we are producing on the farm offers us one of the best markets in the world. The market of the United States is an exporting market, and I will prove to you before I sit down that instead of the United States being a great consuming market like the German Empire it is a market that is exporting large quantities of the very products that we are asked to send into the United States. On the other hand here is the German market which is the best market in the world, but one, and we are not in anything like the favourable position that we were in with regard to that market in 1896, a condition of things which was brought about by the present government. What about the Japanese Treaty? I have not time to go into this question, but the hon. gentleman knows what the outcome is of the Japanese Treaty. Then, take the French Treaty, and I ask what good has it done to us? Look up the trade and navigation returns, and find the different kinds of things we are sending into France and see what little advantage this country has derived from the French Treaty. It was brought about in a manner that must have been humiliating to the Minister of Customs and the Minister of Finance. We remember the boastful way in which it was given to the people of Canada in the first place, and then we remember those hon. gentlemen coming down to the House, and having to take back, for instance, the entry of cattle into the French market. As a result of the position in which these gentlemen were placed they were only able to get into that country a very small amount of goods from the Dominion of Canada in return for the splendid concessions they gave to France. What was the outcome of it? Last year the United States held the big stick over them with reference to the French Treaty and obtained large concessions the ultimate outcome of which was our friends going over to Washington and entering into the present commercial arrangements. We have now a Yankee agreement, but the Yankee agreement opens the door to many other countries as well, and when these gentlemen on the government side of the House argue in favour of this agreement as regards dairy products, like Mr. ARMSTRONG.

my good friend from the island, (Mr. War-burton), they want to take into consideration that last year in the month of January 5,000 boxes of butter came from Argentina into the Montreal market, and the price of butter dropped from 25 to 19 cents a pound in a few days. What about the fact that within the last ten days, in this very year, 2,000 boxes of New Zealand butter came into British Columbia? What position is our country going to be in when the door is open to all these lands to ship their dairy products in? If you investigate this question you will find that in opening our doors to these countries, as you are compelled to open them now, you are going to make of Canada a dumping ground for butter, cheese and dairy products from other countries.

Not only that, 'but Australian mutton will supply the western market to. a very great extent. Under the most favoured nation treaty Canada will have to extend the same tariff advantages she gives to the United States to the following countries : Argentine, Austro-Hungary, Bolivia, Columbia, Denmark, Japan, Norway, Russia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Venezuela, and in addition, by special arrangement with Canada, France and Germany must also share in the concessions. We are opening the markets of Canada to make them a dumping ground for the products of these countries. My good friend from Prince Edward Island (Mr. Warlburton) spoke of the wonderful advantages the people of Canada would have in farm and dairy products toy this arrangement. Does he know that we imported into Canada from the United States last year $52,597 worth of poultry, and that we exported only $3,576 worth to the United States; does he know that our imports of potatoes from the United States were valued at $213,554, and our exports to the United States $36,770. Does the hon. gentleman know that $177,577 worth, or 750,000 dozens of eggs came last year from the United States to Canada, and that we were only able to send back there 39,910 dozens valued at $12,596? Let the hon. gentleman remember these figures and perhaps he will not have such a high idea of the advantages we will receive in the matter of dairy and farm products. We would expect a large quantity of wood pulp go to the United States, tout we must remember it is manufactured to some extent here, and last year 30,627 pounds came into Canada from the United States while 4,224,000 went from Canada to the United States. Of newsprint 234,000 pounds came to Canada wnile 1,600,000 pounds went to the United States, and the people of the United States buy it simply because they can't help themselves. Then, I can tell my hon. friend (Mr. Warburton) that the horse men of western Ontario are deathly opposed to this reciprocal arrange-

ment, because they know it will take away from them, the northwest market which is very profitable, and it will allow a class of horses to be imported into this country which should never foe allowed to come here. I know my hon. friend (Mr. War-burton) is (big enough and broad enough, when he knows the facts to admit that he is wrong, and to vote against this reciprocal arrangement, and 1 think he will be ready for that admission when I tell him that 6,604 horses came from the United States last year, and that Canada sent only 2,615 in return. Then again, gentlemen who support the government have told us of the wonderful advantage the cheese men are to have from this reciprocal arrangement. Let them remember that a couple of years ago the Dominion produced over 300,000,000 pounds of cheese, and that our exports of cheese to the mother land were valued at $25,000,000, we supplying 60 per cent of the British market. Let them remember the danger there is to our trade in that market from this reciprocal arrangement, and then perhaps they will not have such a high opinion of it. 330496,ca.proc.d.1911-02-16.3.5.19,1911-02-16,intervention,,,,WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH UNITED STATES.,CANNOT BOTH BE RIGHT.,,Who is paying the interest, that is all right. But you must have a higher rate of interest if you are going on with your reciprocity deal because you will interfere with these transportation companies, with these great cities in the west; and instead of them building up and becoming the great manufacturing centres, you will have the people of the west fixing their eyes on the city of Chicago or New York and doing their trading in that direction, because you can depend on it if our wheat and cattle and other farm products go to Chicago these cars are not coming back empty. These cars will come back filled with manufactured products to supply the people of our great west and these supplies will not come over the Canadian railroads. The Minister of Customs knows that he can go on to Regina and will find that the bonds of the street railway there are held in the old land. In Calgary practically the whole city is owned by Britons and run largely by them. Whose money is it that is building up Vancouver? Is it United States money that is building up these great enterprises in our western cities? No, it is the money of the mother land. Come to Toronto, Montreal, Quebec or Halifax, and you will find British capital invested everywhere.

Prominent men of the United States have already distinctly and emphatically said that this step is in the direction of annexation and no other. They are entering into it with that consideration in view Mr. ARMSTRONG.

apparently and I have heard some men go so far to say that the Minister of Customs and even the Minister of Finance had some vague messages of this kind put up to them while they were in the United States. But let me tell the Minister of Customs that as far as British capital is concerned, there is great agitation about this important question. British capitalists have invested in our railways and financial institutions and undertakings to an enormous extent.

We also find that in the last few years 225 American firms have invested $320,000,000 in Canada. Does the Minister of Customs expect that these gentlemen are going to continue to invest in the Dominion of Canada if you are taking steps towards free trade? Where is the manufacturer who would leave a market of 90,000,000 people for a market of 7,000,000 and expect to improve his position unless the seven millions market was protected for him? The Minister of Customs knows that and by this Bill he has given a serious setback to the bringing in of American capital for investment in the Dominion of Canada. If the manufacturer established on this side he would live in fear of the 90,000,000 market being taken away from him. So the only hope of permanence for this arrangement lies in political union. Do the people of Canada want it? They do not. The United States has a tariff of 42 per cent against us, while we have one of 26 per cent against them. Let them lower their tariff so that it conforms with our own before they start to talk of trade arrangements. When the United States abrogated the reciprocity treaty Sir John Macdonald enunciated his policy, that policy which to-day gives us the home market for 80 per cent on our products. That national policy is still the trade policy of Canada, it has been the policy for the last fifteen years and the Minister of Customs knows full well that were it not for that policy the splendid prosperity and advancement that we have had in this Dominion would not have been brought about by anything that the present government have undertaken. The free trade Liberal in Canada, it is true, has been told that the tariff has been revised downwards, but the men who make such statements know better and the Minister knows better. $33,000,000 of the goods of our country go free into the United States and $104,000,000 of goods from the United States come free in to the Dominion, and yet the United States are said to be giving us a square deal The Americans were convinced that they would have to make a change in their tariff and to make it downward. A dying congress gave them the opportunity. They offered to open up negotiations with this government and this government, which had been in power fifteen years and was pretty near the jumping off place, joined with the

United States government, which was in the same position, for the purpose of keeping the two in power. Our government said: We must do something to draw the people's attention away from the graft and the corruption which has been rampant in this country during the past fifteen years and from our abortive naval policy. On the other side President Taft was practically a defeated man before he made this reciprocity agreement, but now he is able to go boasting throughout that country of having the advantage over Canada and there can be no doubt that he will be reelected on this measure.

330498,ca.proc.d.1911-02-16.3.5.21,1911-02-16,9b9087eb-6add-462b-bc28-48898b45eb69,ca.m.4640,Mr. ARMSTRONG.,,WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH UNITED STATES.,CANNOT BOTH BE RIGHT.,,Let me tell the Minister of Customs that when the people of Canada come to thoroughly understand the workings of this scheme, they will never forgive the government for having put it into execution. The government are making themselves servants to the men at Washington. They are taking away our right to making our own tariff. Let the Minister of Customs listen to the utterances of some of the prominent men of his own party. Why did he not listen to the Hon. G. W. Ross who said that reciprocity would be the ruin of Canadian industry? Had I the time I could quote statement after statement by prominent Liberals against this agreement. Take again the position assumed by the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) with regard to this deal, and also that of Senator McMullen. Go to your hanks throughout the Dominion, and I understand there is only one general manager of a (bank in the whole country who is in favour of this proposition. The others are distinctly and emphatically opposed to it.

The motto ' Leave well enough alone ' has been quoted here to-day, and it is one well worth keeping in mind. The United States are the most aggressive competitors we have, and yet we are entering into a pact with them. We have had gentlemen from the west say : Let us sell in Chicago and New York. But what then would be the use of our building the Hudson Bay railway at a cost of $50,000,000 or the Georgian Bay canal at a cost of $100,000,000 or the new Welland canal, or the Grand Trunk Pacific? Why should we pledge the credit of the people to the extent of over $300,000,000 to build that great transcontinental railway, if the producers in our great west are going to send their products to Chicago and New York? What is the good of our improving our transportation facilities east and west, or of our building the Hudson Bay railway if we are to deal with Chicago and New York?

Let us see what has been our expenditure on railways up to 1910. The federal government has expended $427,000,000 ; the provincial governments, $36,000,000; the municipalities, $18,000,000. In addition tbe various governments' federal and provincial, have granted in aid of railway construction no less than 55,000,000 acres of the public domain.

Then there is no permanency .to this arrangement. The Finance Minister said it was not a binding agreement, and if after reasonable trial it was found unsatisfactory we could change it. But if you pass this agreement and have it in force even for only a short space of time, you will do untold injury to our people. Our financial institutions do not want it ; our transcontinental railways do not want it. If this deal goes through our great transcontinental railway will be but a sink hole for the wealth of our country. Our trade and shipping will be done by the Yankees because the cars and boats which carry the wheat south will not come back empty. We were a happy and contented people before this tariff matter developed, our cities were alive with prosperity, but today Canadians and the Canadian press are appealing to the premier to stay these arrangements. They are appealing to him to restore confidence in our industries, to restore confidence in the old land from which we borrow money in large quantities, to restore confidence in the money market, to restore confidence in our railways and transportation lines. Canadian enterprises and corporations must borrow abroad. They do not borrow from the United States. You are injuring the credit of the loan companies and financial institutions of Canada. The insurance companies take the same position. Railways and transportation companies declare, as far -as they dare without prejudicing their stock against it.

Our policy should ibe closer trade relations between Canada and the whole empire, because the 450,000,000 people in the British Empire are the greatest consumers of our natural products. We have' the best granary in the empire, and it is to be taken away and handed over to the Americans. Our trade will go through American instead of Canadian ports. By drawing nearer to the United States, Canada will set her foot on the road to separation from Great Britain.

Let us look for a few minutes at our trade from 1856 to 1866 under the old reciprocity treaty. I have here the figures, showing Canada's trade from 1856 to 1866, under the old reciprocity arrangement. Canada's total imports in 1854 amounted to $40,529,325. These dropped in 1858 to $29,078,527. Canada's total exports in 1854 amounted to $21,249,308. In 1858 they amounted to $22,029,565. In 1865, the year before the abrogation of the treaty, Canada's aggregate exports were $39,607,919 and her total imports amounted to $44,620,469. Two years after the abrogation of the treaty, in 1868, Canada's exports were $44.000,000, and her imports, $57,000,000; in two years an increase of $5,000,000 in her exports and of $18,000,000 in our foreign trade. During the life of the treaty we sacrificed our St. Lawrence ports and route. Shipments to and from Great Britain were sent and received by Oswego, Buffalo, and New York. The exports from Montreal and Quebec fell 33 per cent in one year. And what are the figures to-day ? Our exports amounted in 1910 to $301,358,529, and our imports to $391,852,692. What about the flour milling industry? In Ontario we have over 300 flour mills, and they are all opposed .to this agreement. They believe it will, to a large extent, transfer the milling industry to the United States. There is no question that ,it will transfer the large mills to the United States. Food prices will be raised to the working men through the trusts and the corporations that will control the food of the people who consume them. _ The reduction on manufactured articles is an important one to many of these industries; thus it will stop the American manufacturers from locating in Canada to a great extent. You must remember that labour in the United States is, on the whole, much cheaper than Canada, on the whole. In the city of New York to-day you will find 50,000 men crying for bread. In the city of Pittsburg you will lind 30,000 men working at $1.25 a day, wages that our working men would not care to accept. We place the making of our tariff in the hands of the American Congress. What about the butter industry? I told the minister of the large amount of butter coming into the Dominion from New Zealand and other countries, lowering the price of our product. Cold storage and the transportation of these products will be demoralized. It is my privilege to be president of one of the largest butter factories in the Dominion of Canada. Last year, if we had made all the cream into butter that we received, we would have Mr. ARMSTRONG.

made over 350,000 pounds of creamery butter. But we only made 185,000 pounds, because, during a portion of the year, we shipped the cream to the other side and got a good price for it. But that good price only continued for a small portion of the year, and we found that we could make more money for the farmers by making that 185,000 pounds in our own factories. You can depend upon it that the butter industry of the Dominion of Canada will be seriousiy interfered with if this arrangement goes into effect.

You will find the salt and cheap butters of the United States coming into Canada, and filling our market and supplying it to a very great extent. Oleomargarine and the process butters of the United States have full sway in that country, and there is no doubt that if this government will allow all sorts of cheap butters in the Dominion of Canada they are going to undermine' the great butter industry of this country. If you undermine it here you undermine it in the markets of the world, because our butter sells for a good deal more than United States butter on the British market. Our cheese and dairy products command a higher price than United States exports of these same products in the markets of the world. Take the fish industry of our great lakes; the Americans own today the great fishing boats and Canadians will continue to eat the small fish, pike and whatever is left as we have in the past, and our choice fish will go to feed the Yankees. The Canadian bacon hog has gained a record which it has taken years to bring up to the market standard will disappear and this arrangement will leave the market open for the American animal. There are few constituencies in the older provinces that are not directly interested in these industries. Take my own riding; you have seriously interfered with two salt industries, two wagon works, six flour mills, ten cheese factories, twenty miles of fruit land along the south short of Lako Huron, six evaporator works, two canneries, besides many other industries. Cheese and butter factories were built up under British connection. The government assisted them by cold storage and transportation to the extent of something like $600,000 or $700,000. We stand higher in the British market than the Americans in these products. The vegetable industry pays a duty on its coal, glass, fertilizers, implements, &c., and it is asked to compete with the man outside who has all these things at his disposal free. There have been millions invested in this vegetable industry all over Canada. In fruit and vegetables it is always harder for a northern country to compete with the south. American fruit will arrive several weeks before ours is ripe and by the time the Canadian fruit is ready the consumer has tired of that certain fruit and will wish

some other kind that the United States will supply; so, the Canadian farmer will walk at the tail end and get the glut prices for the fruit if he can sell it at all. With regard to early vegetables the same condition obtains. In Ontario there are 57,000 acres given up to the growing of vegetables,

column2: acres to fruit and 500,000 in the whole Dominion. It requires years to develop a fruit farm. Fruit men are developing our natural resources just the same as any other line of industry and the industry is one which is launched on the sea of doubt. Fruit men are compelled to pay tribute to every other industry. Our western trade will be demoralized if we cannot ship into that country. From the Niagara district in 1904 a sample car was sent. It was followed in 1905 by 25 cars, in 1906 by 264 cars, sent from one shipping point, and in 1910 by 600 cars. It is expected that

cars will represent the shipment of fruit this year to that western country. For every dollar that United States people spend on Canadian fruit we spend $22 on theirs. There is an investment of $150,000,000 in the fruit industry of Canada, and there are 30,000,000 bearing trees. It takes from eight to ten years to get returns and ten acres of orchard will employ as much labour as one hundred acres of wheat. Even with the present duty the United States have made a dumping ground of our markets. The fruit growing industry is a great natural asset, it gives a large amount of traffic to the railroads and consumes the product of box, barrel and basket factories besides supplying canneries, cold storage plants, &c. The prices that the fruit men receive for their products depend upon the time they can be marketed. You will turn the fruit men over to the American trusts to handle their goods and you can depend upon it that in so far as the consumers in Canada are concerned they will not get cheaper fruits. Canada imported from the United States last year $4,634,268 worth of fruits of which $3,428,722 were free. I would like to place a few statistics with regard to this fruit industry on ' Hansard ' because I come from a district that is developing into a most important fruit producing country. At the little town of Forest 55,000 trees are sold to be planted this coming spring. At another place they will plant about 30,000 trees, a large number of them peach trees.
